text: Day one as CEO. Your assistant sends over your calendar: meetings from 7:00 a.m. to 10:45 p.m., lunch is "5 min, in the elevator." Approve it?
Your office door already has a sign with your name and "Chief Executive Officer." The letters are gold and slightly crooked. Redo it on the company's dime?
The guard at the entrance asks for your badge out of habit. It's in your other jacket. Twenty employees are queuing behind you. What now?
The head of strategy brings a five-year strategy. 214 slides, and the last one says "Summary: grow." Approve or send it back?
An investment banker suggests taking the company public in eighteen months. He talks fast, smiles a lot and has already shown you a slide with a rocket. Start preparing?
left: Let's go, the rocket sold me
right: Get the house in order first

text: The CFO whispers that going public needs three years of clean accounts. You have two clean ones, and the third is "more of an art project." Your move?
In the evening the press secretary asks for your official photo for the website. All you've got is a party shot of you in reindeer antlers. Book a photographer?
At dinner your family asks what changed after the promotion. You answer honestly: "Now it's always my fault." Your kid wants to stick that on the fridge. Allow it?
right: Veto: I'm not CEO at home

text: Your calendar shows "Meeting about meetings" at 8:00. You set it up yourself six months ago, back when you were a deputy. Go?
The head of investor relations wants you to learn "the company story in 90 seconds" for investors. The current version lasts seven minutes and starts in 1998. Cut it?
Your driver offers to take the long route "so you have time to think." The short way is twenty minutes, the long one fifty. Which way?
left: The long way, I need to think
right: The short way, people are waiting

text: A business reporter wants an interview "about your first month." He sent questions ahead, and number three is "Why are you better than your predecessor?" Agree?
The retired former CEO calls in the evening "just to see how you're doing." In an hour he says "I'd have done it differently" three times. Keep listening?
At 7:15 a.m. the cleaner finds you in your office: "The last CEO never came in this early. Didn't last long either." Compliment or warning?
The chief accountant brings papers to sign. The stack is as thick as a loaf of bread. A sticky note on top: "No need to read, all checked." Sign blind?
HR suggests you eat in the staff canteen once a week "to be closer to people." The cooks are already setting a separate table with a name card. How to handle it?
right: Eat in your office as before

text: The personal trainer the board gifted you texts: "You've missed six workouts out of six." He's paid up for a year. Go to the seventh?
right: Gift the sessions to your deputies

text: The front desk asks how to answer callers: "The CEO is in a meeting" or "The CEO is busy." You genuinely are always in a meeting. Which one?
The executive meeting is in its second hour. Everyone is waiting for you to speak, and you're waiting for anyone else to. The silence is ringing. Who blinks first?
At 9:40 p.m. your assistant asks if she can go home. You didn't know she stays as long as you do. What do you say?
Your speechwriter sends the shareholders' meeting speech. It includes "we are like a family," and in brackets: "(pause for tears)." Keep it?
At the shareholders' meeting, an elderly shareholder asks the question you dreaded: "Do you actually use our products yourself?" You don't. Your answer?
A shareholder who owns exactly one share speaks for twenty minutes about the logo color. The limit is three minutes. The chair looks at you. Cut him off?
After the shareholders' meeting a queue forms "for a quick word." Twelve people, each with their own quick word. Your driver has been waiting an hour. Stay?
An industry analyst publishes a morning note: "The new CEO is a dark horse." The stock dips slightly. PR asks whether to respond.
The sales director asks you, "for old times' sake," to leave his department alone for a year. You two started out as interns together. Your answer?
Your phone shows 147 unread emails, all marked "urgent." It's 11 p.m. Things look better in the morning, but emails don't know proverbs. Tackle them?
PR hired a stylist. He suggests a "confident leader" look: a turtleneck, non-prescription glasses and a slower walk. Go for it?
The strategy facilitator hands every director a building-block set and asks them to build "the company in five years" in 20 minutes. The CFO builds a safe, sales a rocket. What do you build?
Strategy offsite out of town. After lunch everyone is drowsy, and there are six more hours of "brainstorming" on the agenda. The facilitator looks at you. Carry on?
Evening at the offsite. Your deputy suggests "informally" discussing which directors should be replaced. Everyone is sitting around the campfire. Join in?
Your assistant found a 15-minute gap in your schedule and asks how to fill it. Six requests already, from the marketing director to your dentist. Who gets it?
A warehouse worker ends up in the elevator with you and freezes. Eight floors to go. You can stay silent, or ask how things are. Which?
The warehouse worker from the elevator emails you three pages about warehouse problems. Half is true, half is about his manager. Reply?
Marketing wants to put you in a company ad: "The CEO tries the product in person." The shoot is at 6 a.m. on Saturday. Agree?
The lawyer brings an 80-page contract with the investment bank. You need to understand it by evening. He offers "a one-page summary." Which do you trust?
Your kid asks you to come to the school play on Thursday at 5 p.m. That's when you have a call with investors from three countries. What do you do?
The board chair sends you a book, "100 Habits of Great Leaders," with a note: "See chapter 7." Chapter 7 is "Get up at 4:30." Give it a try?
The CFO asks you to approve your own expense budget. The amount makes even you uncomfortable. Cut it in half?
In the evening your inner voice asks: "What did you actually lead today?" You go through 14 meetings and can't recall a single decision. What now?
left: Write down three decisions for tomorrow

text: A courier delivers a huge bouquet "from suppliers, congratulating you on the appointment." The card adds modestly: "We hope to renew our contract." Accept it?
The CIO wants to give you a "smart office": voice-controlled lights, blinds and music. It costs as much as renovating the canteen. Go for it?
Your spouse reminds you that you promised a vacation "as soon as you become CEO." You did. The calendar says "Q3 next year." What do you say?
right: Ask for a bit more patience

text: Your assistant books a daily 30-minute "thinking time." An hour later the CFO takes it, labeled "urgent, this IS the thinking." Give it up?
Your first town hall. An anonymous question: "Are you here for long?" 300 people wait for the answer. What do you say?
The press secretary sends a list of topics you must never joke about in public. It's longer than the list of topics you can talk about at all. Follow it?
The plant director invites you to "see how it all works." It's a three-hour drive. Your assistant says that day is "fully booked." Go?
At the plant the shop foreman asks you to press the start button on the new line. Photographers everywhere. The button is clearly decorative; the line is already running. Press it?
On the way back from the plant your driver says his daughter graduates tomorrow, and he'd like the day off. You need to be at the airport at 7 a.m. Your call?
left: Let him go, take a taxi
right: Ask him to drive, then leave

text: An invitation to give a keynote at an industry forum: "The Future of the Industry." The organizers write: "No slides, just inspire." Accept?
The banker sends the IPO roadshow schedule: six cities in five days, twenty meetings a day. "Sleep" isn't on it. Sign off?
right: Bargain for one day of sleep

text: Roadshow morning. Seventh investor meeting of the day, and you catch yourself telling the same joke for the third time in an hour. To the same people?
An investor from a big fund asks in the first three minutes: "Why shouldn't I just buy your competitor?" How do you open?
You have 12 minutes between roadshow meetings. You can eat, call home, or reread the numbers. Not enough time for all three. Which one?
Your IR head points out that in the roadshow script your answer on risks lasts nine seconds, and on opportunities nine minutes. Investors noticed. Rewrite?
Late evening at the hotel, you realize you've given the pitch 34 times and you're no longer sure what your company is called. Eight more meetings tomorrow. Now what?
The roadshow hotel mixed up the rooms: your CFO got the suite and you got the room by the elevator. The CFO offers to swap. Swap?
The banker says the order book is three times oversubscribed. You could raise the IPO price, but the first days of trading will be jittery. Raise it?
Employees ask whether they can buy company shares at the IPO. The lawyers say it's possible, but it's a month of paperwork. Set it up?
Legal warns that before the IPO you're in a "quiet period." You can't say anything extra about the company. Not to a neighbor in the elevator. Not even to your mom. How do you live?
Mom calls in the evening: "The neighbor says your firm is being sold. Is it true? Should I buy shares?" One more week of quiet period. What do you tell her?
right: Explain how a stock exchange works

text: First day of trading. The exchange invites you to ring the ceremonial bell. Suit ready, speech ready, you — not so much. Ring it?
right: Have the whole team ring it

text: First hour of trading: shares up 12%, down 8%, up again. You check the chart every 40 seconds. The CFO asks you to stop. Stop?
The press secretary needs three words for the IPO news. PR's version: "A new era of growth." Yours: "We're very tired." Which goes out?
Evening after the IPO. The team wants to celebrate, and tomorrow at 8 a.m. you have your first call with new shareholders. Stay or go?
The morning after the IPO, shares are down 3%. Your phone has 40 "what happened?" messages from people who congratulated you yesterday. Reply?
Legal explains: now that you're public, every phrase you say can move the stock. Even "well, we'll see." Especially "well, we'll see." What about your favorite phrase?
A bank analyst downgraded your stock from "buy" to "hold." The note says: "The CEO looked tired on the roadshow." React?
Your assistant sends next quarter's calendar: now with quarterly earnings calls, broker conferences and "analyst days." Free evenings: two. What now?
In a week you have your first quarterly earnings call. The numbers are good, but one metric unexpectedly slipped. The CFO suggests "not emphasizing it." How do you play it?
On the earnings call an analyst asks something you don't have an answer to. 300 people on the line. The pause is getting long. What do you say?
After the earnings call the CFO writes: "You said 'about 15%,' the report says 14.6%. Legal is nervous." Issue a clarification?
A big fund that bought a stake at the IPO wants a monthly one-on-one with you. There are six such funds. They all want the same. Agree?
An activist fund bought 3% of the shares and sent an open letter: "The company needs a new strategy." It's already in the news. Respond publicly?
The activist fund's representative proposes selling the "non-core" business. That's the division the company started with. Veterans work there. Your answer?
In the evening a thirty-year veteran sends you an old photo of the first workshop. The caption: "We're counting on you." Rumors of a sale have spread. What do you reply?
A business channel invites you to go live at 7:30 a.m. to discuss "the market after the IPO." Makeup at 6:45. Go?
The board reminds you that after the IPO you need independent directors. One candidate is your old boss who once passed you over for promotion. Vote yes?
A finance vlogger posts "Five reasons not to buy this company." Reason three: "the CEO's weird haircut." It's going viral. Your move?
The board granted you stock options. HR asks whether to announce it to staff. Regular employees don't get options. Announce?
Legal brings the insider rules: you can't trade the shares for most of the year, and you can't advise anyone when to buy — not even your uncle. Your uncle is calling. Pick up?
At midnight your inner voice whispers: "Check the Asian markets." Your shares don't trade there. The voice insists. Check?
An accountant put all his savings into company shares and now sends you a daily screenshot of the stock price with an emoji. Today it's a crying one. Reply?
left: Advise him not to bet it all

text: The bank sent its IPO fee invoice and a bouquet. The bouquet is noticeably more modest than the invoice. The CFO asks whether to haggle after the fact. Haggle?
A broker invites you to a "Growth Leaders" conference at a warm resort. Twenty meetings in two days and a pool you'll never have time to use. Go?
An evening at the seaside conference. You have a free hour for the first time all week. A swim, or dinner with an important fund. The fund texts: "We're by the pool." Which is it?
Your IR head suggests a professional networking profile with "leadership thoughts" three times a week. She'll write them, you'll sign. Agree?
left: Write one post a week yourself

text: Your first "leadership" post gets a comment from a former classmate: "Remember when you slept through the exam?" The comment has 100 likes, your post 20. What now?
Your assistant plans your day to the minute: "9:07 coffee, 9:09 call, 9:21 smile in the corridor." The smile item bothers you. Strike it?
Your assistant ran the numbers: 62% of your time goes to meetings about other meetings. She proposes cancelling every third one. Risk it?
Your assistant is off for two weeks. She left an 18-page "how to survive without me" guide and a number she says you "can call, but shouldn't." Call her?
First morning without your assistant. You don't know where your first meeting is, what the calendar password is, or who "Igor, 9:30, important" might be. What now?
"Igor, 9:30, important" turns out to be a marketing intern who waited six months for a slot to pitch you an idea. The idea is meh. But he was so excited. How do you respond?
Your assistant is back from vacation and finds that in two weeks you moved 40 meetings, 12 of them to the same slot. She silently opens her laptop. Apologize?
Security suggests you get a bodyguard after the IPO: "You're a public figure now." He'd follow you even to the canteen. Agree?
Your new bodyguard stands outside the meeting room. Staff are afraid to come in even with coffee. Half the attendees are missing. What do you do?
left: Dismiss the guard on this floor

text: A neighbor saw you in the news as "that CEO" and now tells you every day in the elevator what's wrong with your product. Eighteen floors. What do you do?
Your spouse watches your interview and notes: "You said 'our family' about the company and forgot to mention ours." How do you react?
The board wants to move the shareholders' meeting to 8 a.m. Saturday "so it doesn't disrupt the work week." Shareholders are grumbling; staff would have to come in. Back it?
The board secretary asks you to read the 70-page minutes of the shareholders' meeting by evening. You were at the meeting. But "read" has to be honest. Read it?
Live radio at 7:10 a.m. The host opens with: "Is it true you sleep four hours a night?" It's not, but it sounds impressive. Your answer on air?
left: "I sleep eight, and so should you"

text: Before a TV slot the makeup artist wants to "take the tiredness off your face." Ten minutes later you look rested but slightly orange. Air in five minutes. Wash it off?
left: Wash it off, go as is

text: A business journalist puts a recorder on the table: "Let's skip the press releases, talk like humans." His last "talk like humans" cost two executives their jobs. How do you talk?
At the end the journalist turns off his recorder: "Between us, what do you think of your main competitor?" The recorder is off. The phone in his pocket isn't. Answer?
In the evening the press secretary sends the interview text for approval. It has you saying things you never said, but they sound smarter than you. Keep them?
The interview runs with the headline "CEO: We're ready for tough decisions." Staff in the company chat ask whether that means layoffs. Explain?
A popular business podcast invites you for a three-hour "unedited" recording. Audience: a million people, half of them your customers. Go?
Two hours into the podcast the host asks: "Have you ever wanted to quit it all?" You did — yesterday. Admit it to a million listeners?
In the evening you read the podcast comments. A thousand nice ones and one: "Boring as an earnings report." You've been thinking about that one for twenty minutes. What now?
PR asks you to approve "media training": two days drilling answers to awkward questions. The coach promises you'll stop saying "kind of." Agree?
The media coach teaches you "bridging": answer any question with "That's an important question, but let's talk about our mission." Use it?
On live TV the anchor shows a chart: your prices rose 20% in a year. Close-up camera. You feel your eyebrow twitch. What do you say?
By evening a still of your twitching eyebrow is a meme. Even your employees are sharing it with the caption "when someone asks about the deadline." How do you react?
right: Ask for it to be taken down

text: An agency sends a "CEO reputation index" in the morning: you're 14th out of 50. Your predecessor was 9th a year ago. The board already has a copy. What now?
A crisis consultant offers to prepare statements for 30 possible scandals "preventively." Cost: half a year of a department's salaries. Order it?
An angry customer posts a video of your product breaking in his hands. Millions are watching. Sales suggests you call him personally. Call?
In the evening you call the customer from the video. He doesn't believe he's talking to the CEO and demands you name his order number. You don't know it. Now what?
The press secretary proposes a rule: no interviews before 10 a.m., "because in the mornings you tell the truth." Unclear if that's a compliment. Adopt it?
A photographer shooting a business magazine cover asks you to "look into the distance as if you can see the future." All you see is the air conditioner. Forty takes. More?
The magazine sends the cover for approval. Under your photo: "The CEO Who Never Sleeps." You slept eight hours yesterday. Demand a change?
The rival CEO called your company "yesterday's news" in a morning interview. Journalists are already calling for your reaction. Respond?
At an industry conference you're seated on stage next to the rival CEO. The moderator asks you to "shake hands for the future of the industry." The room waits.
After the conference the rival CEO suggests dinner "with jackets off." You're both tired of the same old questions. Accept?
The staff newsletter goes out with a typo: instead of "Chief Executive" it says "Chief Exuberant." Five hundred people have read it. Fix it?
right: Sign off that way for a week

text: Internal comms is filming your video message to staff. The teleprompter scrolls so fast you sound like an auctioneer. What do you do?
A journalist you know texts in the evening: "An unpleasant story about your company comes out tomorrow. Want to comment by 11 p.m.?" It's 10:40. Answer?
The morning article: "Employees complain of overwork." It quotes an anonymous staffer who sounds suspiciously like something you said in the elevator. What now?
The comms director suggests "fixing the reputation" with an article about how you personally mentor interns. You don't mentor interns. Yet. What now?
In the evening your kid shows you your eyebrow meme: "Is this you? Everyone in class knows you!" Your kid seems proud. You, less so. What do you say?
Your assistant suggests a monthly live Q&A on the intranet. No filter on questions. Brave enough?
At your first live Q&A, the top-voted question: "Why is it buckwheat in the canteen again?" You prepared to talk strategy. The chat demands buckwheat. Answer?
In the canteen that evening the chef comes over: "I watched your Q&A. We make buckwheat because you love it. Your predecessor told us so." What now?
PR suggests posting your morning runs "for the energetic leader image." You don't run. But sneakers can be bought. Start?
Your first morning run. At kilometer three you're overtaken by one of your own company's couriers with a full delivery bag, who greets you cheerfully. What do you do?
Your fitness tracker reports in the evening: "640 steps today, 11 hours sitting." It suggests you "stand up and stretch." You're on a board call. Stand?
Your assistant ordered you a "productivity smoothie" of spinach, celery and something blue. It sits on your desk staring at you. Drink it?
You get home at 10:30 p.m. Everyone has eaten; your plate is under a lid with a note: "For the CEO." Your family's joking. Or are they?
left: Promise to make it to dinner

text: 11 p.m. You open your laptop "for five minutes" to check one number. Next time you look up, it's 1:15 a.m. You never found the number. What about tomorrow?
Your driver suggests audiobooks in the car "instead of news about yourself." He's picked a 40-hour detective novel. Listen?
For the first time in a month you go out for lunch to a café near the office. At the next table, your employees are discussing you. So far, positively. So far. Stay?
At an after-work café you run into a group of analysts. They invite you over "for five minutes." They clearly have questions saved up. Sit down?
A new hire on his first day asks you in the corridor where the "Baikal" meeting room is. He doesn't know who you are. You could walk him there, but you're late. What do you do?
The new hire you walked to the meeting room finds out who you are and posts in chat: "The CEO is all right!" Now eight more newbies want a walk. Agree?
After the town hall the hall cleaner gathers the question cards nobody got to ask. Sixty of them. He hands you the stack: "Seems a shame to bin them." Take them?
right: Ask him to pass them to HR

text: The receptionist notices you've worn the same jacket three days running and discreetly leaves a dry cleaner's card on your desk. Hint taken?
Facilities gave you a parking spot right by the entrance. It used to be the staff bike rack. The cyclists say nothing, but they stare. What now?
left: Give it back to the bikes

text: 3 a.m. You're lying awake rehearsing an answer to a question that might be asked at a meeting in two weeks. Get up and write it down?
left: Get up and write it down

text: In the evening someone who heard your podcast writes: he'd quit his profession, but after your story decided to go back. He asks for advice. Reply?
The comms director proposes a morning ritual: read the daily "What They're Saying About Us" digest. It's 40 pages. Read it?
A major shareholder sends you an article titled "CEOs Who Talk Too Much," with the note "Just an interesting read." Is that a hint?
The CCO drops by at 7:50 and casually asks who'll be your successor "in a couple of years." He's clearly talking about himself. Your answer?
The CFO and CCO are fighting over whose number goes in the annual report. Each came to you separately to say the other "doesn't understand the business." How do you settle it?
Your first deputy sends an evening "idea to mull over": split the company in two, with him running one half. Thirty slides. Read it tonight?
right: Discuss it face to face tomorrow

text: HR asks you to approve a new org chart. Every director gained one direct report; you gained three. Approve it?
right: Send it back: I have enough

text: The sales director brings a plan to grow revenue 40%. It needs twice the headcount and your personal signature on a promise to the board. Sign it?
At the leadership meeting the marketing director says: "No offense, but we all want your chair." Everyone laughs except you. Your reply?
The marketing director sends you an evening link to a CEO opening at another company: "Think it'd suit me?" Is that a request for advice or a threat?
Your assistant says three directors each asked for "ten minutes in private." Each topic is "confidential." Probably the same thing. How do you see them?
left: One by one, ten minutes each

text: The three "confidential" topics turn out to be one: who gets the new office with the river view. One office, three directors. How do you decide?
left: Turn it into a meeting room
right: Give it to the KPI winner

text: At the end of the day the CFO admits he's had an offer from a competitor. He'll stay "if you personally ask." Ask him?
The board wants a succession plan by quarter-end: who replaces you "just in case." Naming your most ambitious deputy would give him wings. Who goes in?
The CIO demands a seat at all your strategy sessions: "Digital is everything." The other directors think "everything" is them. Let him in?
left: Invite him to all of them

text: The head of operations says he won't attend meetings "where we discuss slides instead of machines." He's half right. What now?
left: Excuse him from half of them

text: In the leadership chat your deputy announces a decision you haven't made, "as agreed with the CEO." You agreed nothing. How do you handle it?
left: Correct him in the group chat

text: The general counsel wants promotion to "chief legal and ethics officer." Ethics in his department so far means a "Quiet please" sign. Promote him?
Every director spends exactly five minutes on their wins. Nobody mentions problems. Forty minutes to go. What do you do?
The head of strategy proposes a "culture of failure": every month directors share their mistakes. They suggest you go first. Agree?
At the first "failure culture" session you shared a mistake. By morning it's being retold by the smokers' corner with details that never happened. Continue?
You hired a new marketing director. In his first week he sent you 27 ideas, three of them about renaming the company. How do you cool him down?
right: Ask for a month of quiet

text: The new marketing director and the veteran sales director haven't spoken since day three. Their joint project is stuck. Call them in?
At lunch the two directors are finally talking. About how badly a third director performs. He's sitting at the same table. What now?
HR proposes a 360-degree review for the leadership team, including you. All direct reports will rate you anonymously. Do it?
The 360 results are in. Your lowest score is "listens to others." Comment: "Interrupts even people who agree." Discuss it with the team?
The board paid for an executive coach. In session one he asks you to describe your ideal workday. You describe a day with no meetings. The coach goes silent. Continue?
Your coach's assignment: a week without making a single decision for your reports. At 9:15 a director asks you what color the packaging should be. Decide?
The director you told to "decide yourself" decided. The packaging is now lime green with purple stars. The board is in shock. What now?
The CFO writes late: "You asked not to be disturbed, but the CCO is handing out unapproved discounts again." Raise it at tomorrow's meeting?
The CFO's assistant brings you a coffee "just because" and drops a folder on your desk: "to sign, urgent, the CFO asked." Sign?
The sales director asks you to visit the biggest client in person: "He wants to see the top person." Nine-hour flight, forty-minute meeting. Go?
Nine-hour flight to the client. You're in business, the sales director's in economy. He's stoically silent. The steward offers to seat you together. What do you do?
Your biggest client opens the meeting: "I thought the CEO would be taller." Your sales director turns to stone. How do you continue?
The client wants a 20% discount "for coming in person." Behind your back the sales director signals "yes." The CFO would signal "no." Your answer?
After the meeting the sales director says "thanks for coming" for the first time in years. You're both at the airport; the flight is delayed three hours. How do you spend them?
Your assistant suggests starting each day with a 15-minute standup with the directors, like developers do. They're already joking about "CEO scrum." Do it?
The "15-minute" standup with the directors is at 50 minutes. Each says "quickly" and talks for ten. You're late for your next meeting. How do you stop it?
left: Put a timer on the table

text: In the evening your deputy suggests you "take a break" — two weeks off: "I'll cover." The offer is suspiciously generous. Go?
Day one of vacation. At 7:30 a.m. your deputy sends a photo of himself at your desk: "Great place to work!" React?
You're on the beach and your phone buzzes every ten minutes with "FYI" emails. None need action, all demand attention. Turn them off?
An evening on vacation. Your kid wants a bedtime story, and you find yourself telling "the three little pigs and their quarterly plan." The kid loves it. Continue?
First morning back from vacation. 900 emails. Your assistant suggests deleting anything older than three days: "If it matters, they'll write again." Delete?
While you were away, your deputy held three meetings and cancelled two of your projects. The team is confused. What do you do?
You talk to your deputy privately that evening. He says he wants more responsibility and was "just taking initiative." Your response?
The leadership team proposes a mountain team-building offsite with river rafting, everyone in one boat. The CFO can't swim and won't talk about it. Approve?
At the mountain retreat the facilitator asks the directors to carry you across "the river of trust." It's a knee-deep stream. The directors glance at each other. Lie back?
Evening by the campfire at the retreat. For the first time the CFO talks about something other than numbers. Everyone is listening. Your phone buzzes: the board chair. Answer?
The CIO wants you to personally announce the switch to a new accounting system. "If the CEO says it, nobody will resist." They will. Announce it?
The logistics director is hurt he wasn't invited to the retreat: "I found out from the photos." He really was forgotten. What do you do?
Your assistant says the directors now book you through her instead of just dropping by, because it's "more official." You have 30% more meetings. What now?
The logistics director who missed the retreat sends an evening photo of himself alone in the mountains: "Team-built with myself." How do you respond?
left: Invite the whole team to dinner

text: At 8 p.m. your assistant leaves a printout on your desk: "People you promised to call back this week." 23 names. Call today?
A charity asks the company to become lead partner of a children's library program. The sum is noticeable, and the board doesn't know yet. Sign a letter of intent?
left: Sign, defend it at the board
right: Clear it with the board first

text: The CFO brings three charity budget options: "modest," "sensible" and "same as the competitor." The last is triple the first. Which one?
An evening charity gala. The host suddenly announces: "And now our CEO will run the auction!" You've never run an auction. Go up?
At the charity auction the lot is lunch with you. No bids for a full minute. The room looks at you with pity. What now?
right: Add a factory tour to the lot

text: Lunch with the auction winner: a retiree who saved for six months to win it. He brought a notebook with 40 questions about the company. You have an hour. Answer all?
Staff invite you to a Saturday volunteer park cleanup. You planned to sleep till noon for the first time in a month. Go?
At the park cleanup the PR photographer takes 40 shots while you pick up two candy wrappers. Staff with full trash bags wait for the photo shoot to end. What now?
The press secretary wants a press release: "CEO personally cleans up park." You picked up two wrappers and a bottle cap. Release it?
left: Make it about the whole team

text: Your old school asks you to speak to the graduating class. Topic: "How to become a CEO." You're not quite sure yourself how it happened. Go?
left: Go and tell the honest story

text: After your talk a student asks: "What if I don't want to be a CEO — is that okay?" The teachers are watching. Your answer?
The charity director sends an evening report: your money renovated 14 libraries. At the end, a child's drawing: a CEO in a crown handing out books. Hang it in your office?
right: Give it to the company museum

text: A call-center agent writes to you directly: her team is raising money for a colleague's treatment and asks the company to chip in. The approval process takes three weeks. What do you do?
HR proposes a mutual aid fund: the company doubles every ruble staff donate to each other. The CFO grabs a calculator. Launch it?
A competitor announces a donation twice the size of yours. PR asks in the evening: shall we double ours "so we don't look stingy"? Double it?
An animal shelter asks to bring puppies to the office for a "meet the pups" day. Half the staff are thrilled, one has allergies, the lawyer has questions. Allow it?
left: Allow it in a separate room

text: Puppy day. One puppy has been asleep under your desk for three hours, and you're afraid to move. Investor meeting in ten minutes. Wake him?
In the evening the shelter says the puppy that slept under your desk "has clearly chosen an owner." You don't have time to walk even yourself. Adopt him?
right: Find him an owner at the office

text: HR suggests you mentor interns for an hour a week. Your assistant says the only free hour is Tuesdays at 7 a.m. The interns agree. Do you?
At mentoring, an intern asks: "How do you deal with stress?" You honestly think about it and realize you don't. Your answer?
An intern sends a two-page thank-you after your session. At the end: "Can I list you as my mentor on my résumé?" Agree?
right: Ask him to work a bit first

text: The doorman, here for 25 years, is retiring. HR offers the standard card. He remembers you as an intern. What do you do?
The doorman's farewell. You're asked to say a few words. You planned three, but then remember the night he let you in for your forgotten keys. The speech runs long. Stop?
Every Friday you write a letter to staff. It's 9 p.m. and there's no letter. You could hand it to PR, or write three lines yourself. Which?
You arrive at the plant unannounced at 6:30 a.m., start of the shift. The shift supervisor goes pale and tries to hide a kettle under the desk. What now?
A factory worker tells you to your face: "Directors only show up when something's broken." The foreman tries to lead him away. Your reply?
The evening shift asks permission to hang drawings and family photos in the workshop. Health and safety objects: "It's not standard." Allow it?
Engagement survey: 70% are "proud of the company," but only 12% "know who the CEO is." PR suggests hanging your portrait around. Do it?
You're walking the floors. On the fourth, people mistake you for a new hire and ask for help moving a cabinet. It's heavy, you're in a suit. Help?
By evening the office is buzzing about the CEO moving a cabinet. The story has grown: now you carried it down the stairs alone. Correct it?
You decide to spend a day as one of your company's couriers. At 7 a.m. they hand you a backpack, a tablet and 32 addresses. Too late to back out?
At the fifth address a customer recognizes you and starts filming. "The CEO delivered my order in person!" In an hour the video is online. What do you do?
right: Ask him not to post it

text: After your "courier day" you realize the courier app is terrible. It was built by the team the CIO is proudest of. Say so at tomorrow's meeting?
The union rep comes in the morning, not about pay, but asking for decent chairs in the workshop. The chairs cost less than your own. Decide?
The union asks you to attend the staff assembly in person. There'll be awkward questions and two microphones, neither working. Go?
At the staff assembly an older employee stands to thank you for the new chairs. The room applauds. You didn't expect it and don't know what to do with your hands. What do you say?
Your driver's off sick. You take the subway to work for the first time in three years. In the car you spot your company's ad — with a typo. Snap it for marketing?
You're having lunch in the staff canteen. No one sits at your table though the room is full. People hover with trays. What do you do?
The cleaner says staff leave complaint notes on your desk while you're out. She tidies them into a drawer. The drawer is full. Read them?
right: Set up a proper idea box

text: First week of the idea box. Inside: 40 notes. 12 about parking, 8 about coffee, one — a brilliant new product idea. Unsigned. Find the author?
left: Call for the author to step up
right: Pass it to the product team

text: The brilliant idea came from a forklift driver. The product team says they "were thinking the same thing." They weren't. What do you do?
In the evening the forklift driver writes that he's been offered a spot on the product team, but he's scared: "I don't know anyone there." Your advice?
A customer emails in the morning: your support team helped her in the middle of the night when everything broke. She names the agent. What do you do?
The night-shift agent you called admits he's been asking for a day shift for a year. You could fix it with one email. Write it?
A headhunter you know suggests in the evening that you "just chat" about a CEO role at a bigger company. You're six months into the job. Meet?
right: Grab a coffee out of curiosity

text: The company turns 30. PR wants a video of you telling the company story. You've been here five years. Who tells it?
At the anniversary party you're asked to cut a giant logo-shaped cake. The knife is blunt, the cake three tiers tall, 400 staff with phones around. Cut it?
End of the anniversary party. You stand at the exit and shake hands with everyone leaving. All 400 of them. After 150 handshakes your arm goes numb. Keep going?
6:20 a.m. Security calls: a fake "CEO" account has appeared online, handing out "company bonuses" to followers. 3,000 followers already. What now?
The fake "you" online answers customers more politely, faster and funnier than the real you. Customers love it. It'll be removed tomorrow. Learn anything?
In the evening a screenshot of your internal email reaches a journalists' chat. In it you call a project "our little fire." Harmless in context; the screenshot isn't. React?
The security chief offers to find out who leaked the screenshot: "Thirty people got the email. Five minutes and we'll know." Search?
The CFO got an email "from you" asking to urgently wire money to a new supplier. Your signature, your style, even your usual typo. He checks with you. Praise him?
Security ran a mock phishing campaign. 40% of staff clicked the link, including three directors. And you. What do you do with the results?
7 a.m. The press secretary wakes you: a photo of you yawning at a forum under the banner "The Future of the Industry" is in the news. Headline: "The Future Is Bored." Respond?
Legal reports a former partner is suing and telling journalists you "personally promised" him a contract. You met him once at a conference. What do you do?
An investigative reporter sends 15 questions about company procurement. You have 24 hours. Three questions you don't understand; two you understand all too well. How do you respond?
In the evening you find out the "two all-too-clear questions" are true: a procurement manager bought from his brother-in-law's firm for years. Announce before publication?
The board chair texts at 6:45 a.m.: "Saw the procurement story. Why am I reading about it in the paper?" It came out fifteen minutes ago. Respond before the meeting?
The crisis team meets in the "Serenity" room. It's loud. Each director proposes firing someone from a neighbor's department. How do you restore order?
Day three of the crisis. You can't remember your last hot meal. Your assistant silently puts down a bowl of soup and turns off your office light for 15 minutes. Resist?
Quality reports a possible defect in a batch: one in a hundred thousand. Recalling it would cost a quarter's profit. Recall?
After the recall decision the shares drop 6%. An hour later a customer emails: "Thank you for not taking chances with my kids." Forward it to the board?
An anonymous user comments every evening under every company post: "The CEO is incompetent." Posts about the weather, a holiday, the new office. Everywhere. React?
Security found out who the anonymous troll is: an old classmate still sore about a school competition you won. What now?
The company dropped out of the best employers ranking. The reason: employee reviews on a job site. The top review: "Good place, but you never see the CEO." What now?
In the evening you read company reviews on a jobs site. One is about you: "Seems nice, but we've only ever seen the CEO on video." You want to reply. Under your own name?
The morning rumor at the smokers' corner: the company is being sold. You hear it from your driver. It isn't being sold. Yet. Make a statement?
Your assistant brings a printout: "What people said about you online this week." 12 pages. Compliments, and comments about your hair. Read it?
PR asks you to send a photo of your outfit before every public appearance. You're already in pajamas, and tomorrow you're live at 7 a.m. Send one?
Morning TV. The host suddenly asks what a liter of milk costs. You haven't bought milk in six months; your family does. Cameras rolling. Answer?
After the milk question, social media debates whether "the CEO is out of touch." Your assistant suggests a store visit with a camera. Go?
In the evening you buy milk yourself. The cashier recognizes you and says loudly: "Oh, now you know what it costs!" The queue laughs. Your reply?
The CIO reports an overnight hacking attempt. It was repelled, but the hackers left a note: "Tell the CEO his password is weak." Change it?
right: Change it, joke at the meeting

text: IT demands your new password be 20 characters. You forget it in five minutes. Your assistant offers to write it on a sticky note. Write it down?
At the movies someone recognizes you. The person next to you whispers his views on the quarterly results through the whole film. It's a comedy. What do you do?
A major shareholder sends you an article: "Strong CEOs always have polished shoes." Your shoes remember the previous CEO. A hint?
A polling firm publishes a survey: "What animal is the CEO?" The top answer for you is "owl." Good or bad?
left: Put an owl in the logo

text: A warehouse fire at night. No one hurt, but reporters are already filming the smoke. PR wants you on camera at 2 a.m. Go?
left: Go be with the people there

text: The morning after the fire. Warehouse staff stand at the gates, unsure whether to report for their shift. There's no warehouse, but they're expecting pay. What do you tell them?
The insurer says the warehouse payout will take six months and "some contract clauses can be interpreted differently." Legal is ready to sue. Sue?
In the evening you bring the fire station thanks and boxes of food. The chief asks if you could install proper detectors "so we don't meet like this again." Your answer?
Your assistant reports six overlapping meetings today, each marked "critical." Two are with the same people. What now?
Calendar alert: "Lunch break starts in 1 minute." In one minute the bank call starts too. The bank is waiting. So is lunch. Pick one.
left: The bank, lunch in the car

text: In the evening you notice next week has no free hour at all. Even Thursday night has an "Asia call." Cut some?
Your assistant proposes a system: all meetings with you last 25 minutes instead of 30. "Five minutes for walking and bathroom." The directors are outraged at being "trimmed." Do it?
To fit everything in, you hold a walking meeting with the CIO in the corridor. He's explaining system architecture and walks into the water cooler. Change format?
9 p.m. Your assistant sends tomorrow's to-do list. Item one: "Remember what you promised your spouse." You don't remember. Call and ask now?
Your assistant introduces a rule: if someone is three minutes late to a meeting with you, it's cancelled. At 9:03 the board chair hasn't shown up. Cancel?
A partner has moved your meeting for the fifth time, always ten minutes before the start. Your assistant no longer believes he exists. Book a sixth?
Out of the blue, you've got two free hours from 6 p.m. Your assistant is already reaching to fill them. What do you do first?
The board chair asks you to find "half an hour, any day" this week. There's not a half hour in sight. But it's the chair. What do you move?
HR asks you to interview a candidate for her deputy. He's been waiting in reception for 40 minutes because you're on a call. What now?
You get home and realize you drank no water all day. Just coffee, eight cups. Your assistant got you a smart bottle that glows when you forget to drink. It's glowing. Drink?
Alarm at 5:30 a.m. You slept four hours. At 7:00 there's a strategy session you scheduled yourself. Only you can cancel it. Cancel?
Your assistant found a recurring "Lunch with Sergey, every Tuesday" in your calendar — for six months. You don't remember any Sergey. Sergey shows up every Tuesday and waits. What now?
Sergey turns out to be an old mentor you once invited to lunch and forgot. For six months he came every Tuesday, ate in the canteen and left without complaint. What now?
left: Invite him onto an advisory panel

text: The strategy head proposes buying a small startup with "breakthrough technology." Nine people, zero revenue, a very pretty website. Buy it?
The startup founder, in a hoodie and slippers, says he'll sell only if you "share his values." The values are on sticky notes on the wall. Read them?
In the evening the founder writes: "After the deal I want to stay, but with no boss. And no meetings. And no dress code." Agree?
The board wants an answer by Friday: buy the startup or not. Your CFO is 40% for, the CIO 140%. Your call?
Deal closed. On day one the nine startup people arrive with dogs and a projector. Security doesn't know what to do about the dogs. What now?
right: Ask them to leave dogs home

text: A month after the acquisition, your engineers and the startup's developers argue over whose code is better. It's spilled into the company chat with name-calling. Step in?
The CIO wants an AI that writes emails in your name. In the test it signed off to the board chair with "Hugs, your CEO." Deploy it?
The AI built you an "optimal" weekly schedule. It put sleep at 2–5 a.m. and lunch at 4:40 p.m. in the car. Ditch the robot?
In the evening you ask the AI for a town hall speech. It's good, but calls the employees "users" three times. Use it?
right: Swap the word and read it

text: In an anonymous survey staff worry AI will replace them. The top question for you: "Will we be cut?" How do you answer?
A staff retraining program costs as much as three new machines. The CFO notes that machines "at least don't quit." Which do you pick?
In the evening your inner voice asks: "Could an AI replace you?" You recall you spent 80% of today forwarding emails. Worried?
The strategy session opens with an exercise: "Imagine the company no longer exists. Why?" The directors got carried away and have been cheerfully burying the company for half an hour. Stop them?
The facilitator asks for the company mission "in one sentence a grandma would understand." You come up with three paragraphs. A grandma wouldn't get it. What now?
On the phone your grandma states the company mission: "You make useful things and don't cheat people." Shorter and better than anything from the offsite. Propose it?
The board wants a "bolder" strategy. Last time you proposed something bold, they called it "reckless." What do you bring this time?
right: The same, in a bold font

text: A pricey consulting firm delivers its conclusion: "Focus on your key customers." You told them that at the first meeting. Pay?
A young consultant admits to you after the project that he did 80% of the report in one night. He wants to work for you. Hire him?

The business development head proposes entering a neighboring country. Different language, different laws, and "big potential," according to research. How many people there know your brand: zero. Risk it?
At negotiations abroad the partner invites you to the sauna "for a real conversation." It's the custom. You're in a suit with an interpreter. What do you do?
An evening on a trip abroad. The partners invite you to dinner, and you're too tired to speak even your own language. You could plead fatigue. Will they be offended?
You're traveling, eight hours' time difference. At 4 a.m. local time there's a meeting back home. Your assistant set an alarm for 3:30 "just in case." Get up?
Your interpreter translates your jokes word for word. The partners stay silent. Your best logistics joke came out like a threat. Keep joking?
right: Ask him to translate the meaning

text: Your evening flight home is cancelled. The next one is in 14 hours. Your assistant found a private jet: pricey, but you'd be home tomorrow. The board hates private jets. Fly?
The CFO proposes saving money by ending business class for all directors. Including you. The directors are drafting a petition. Your decision?
left: Cut it for all, me included

text: Next year's budget is 4% short. Each director thinks the 4% should come from a neighbor. You're the only one who can decide. How do you cut?
11:10 p.m. You're working on a 40-tab budget spreadsheet. One formula references itself, and the budget grows every time you open it. Call the CFO?
Shareholders want bigger dividends. Directors want bigger investment. Staff want bigger bonuses. The money is the usual amount. Who gets priority?
The board offers you an annual bonus. Meanwhile salaries across the company are frozen. Taking it is fair under your contract, but awkward. Take it?
Your spouse learns from the news that you turned down your bonus. "You could at least have asked me first." Fair. Your reply?
The product team demos a new version. Faster, prettier, and it broke right in your hands during the demo. The team stares at the floor. What do you say?
Marketing wants you to launch the new product on stage, walking out to "epic movie" music. The music's already licensed. Go out?
Launch evening. The product works, but the website crashed under the rush and is down. The CIO asks for two more hours. Customers are posting online. What do you do?
The morning after the crash the CIO hands you his resignation "just in case." He didn't sleep all night; the site is up. What do you do with the letter?
left: Tear it up, send him to bed

text: Sales wants to raise the new product's price by 15%: "If the site crashed, demand must be huge." Logical, and a little cynical. Raise it?
In the evening you read reviews of the new product. A five-star one: "Great, but why is the manual 90 pages?" The lawyers wrote it. Shorten it?
A key supplier announces a 25% price hike this morning. There's an alternative, but switching takes six months. The supplier's CEO wants a one-on-one. Go?
The supplier's CEO opens with: "CEO to CEO. My shareholders are squeezing me too." He's almost in tears. So are you, a little. What do you offer?
You realize the CEOs of your suppliers, clients and even rivals all complain about the same things. Someone proposes a private club "for whining." Join?
The CFO proposes a loan to modernize the plants. High interest, but it pays off in three years. "If nothing goes wrong." Something always goes wrong. Take it?
In exchange for the loan, the bank wants your personal guarantee that you'll hit the plan. Legal says it's "symbolic." It doesn't sound very symbolic. Sign?
In the evening they show you a new machine in the workshop. Veterans eye it like a rival, young workers like a toy. What do you say at the unveiling?
Office rent went up. The CFO suggests moving out of town: half the price, but an extra hour's commute for staff. Move?
right: Move and run a shuttle bus

text: Half the staff want to work from home, half in the office. Directors want everyone in, because "you can see who's working." Your decision?
In the evening you notice you yourself spent only two out of five days in the office — the rest at trips and meetings. Directors are joking about the "hybrid CEO." Respond?
right: Sit in the office to set an example

text: At 8 a.m. your assistant hands you a card: "Today: CFO's birthday, board chair's wedding anniversary, courier Misha's son was born." Who gets congratulated in person?
right: The chair in person, the rest by email

text: Your assistant quietly notes you've called the new sales director by his predecessor's name for three weeks. He doesn't correct you, but he's getting sadder. What now?
Your assistant confesses she's been replying to your birthday messages with emojis in your name for six months. Everyone thinks you're very expressive. Stop it?
Your assistant is off sick. Filling in today: an intern from reception who's terrified of you and double-checks every word. Can you cope?
The intern standing in for your assistant mixed up rooms and led the investors into the staff yoga class. The investors are already on mats. What now?
In the evening the stand-in intern tearfully apologizes for the yoga mix-up. You know the investors loved it and even asked for the class schedule. How do you console him?
Your assistant was promoted and is moving to another department. HR sent three candidates: one speaks five languages, one knows the company inside out, one knows how to calm you down. Which?
Your new assistant asks you to send "your preferences." You realize you've never thought about what you prefer. Except buckwheat. What do you write?
right: Ask her to check with the old one

text: Your new assistant sends tomorrow's schedule at 10 p.m.: "If anything's off, let me know. I'm awake." Is that a warning sign?
left: Ask her not to work nights

text: Morning. Your kid asks to bring you to school for "career day." You'll need to tell the class what you do. In a few words. You don't know how to say it in a few words.
At career day a kid asks: "Do you make anything with your hands?" The firefighter and the chef already showed cool stuff. Your answer?
In the evening your family has a "phones-off dinner." Your phone in the basket by the door has buzzed eight times. Everyone pretends not to hear. Get up?
In the morning a neighbor asks you to sign the building's petition to replace the elevator. "You're a director, they'll listen to you." The management company won't, but he believes. Sign?
The class parents' chat asks "one of the executives" to sponsor the graduation party. Everyone looks at your avatar. It's a cat, but everyone knows whose. What do you do?

The faucet at home is leaking. For the fifth evening you promise to fix it, and for the fifth evening you're on a call. Your spouse called a plumber. He asks you for tools. You don't know where they are.
At your annual check-up the company doctor says: "You should rest more." A minute later your assistant texts: "They're waiting in the meeting room." What do you tell the doctor?
Your lunch is a fifth coffee and a cookie from the meeting room. The CFO sees this and silently puts down a container of his mom's meatballs. Eat?
In the evening you decide to walk home. 40 minutes with no calls. At minute twelve the board chair calls. Pick up?
left: Let it ring, call back later
right: Pick up and talk while walking

text: HR introduced "morning meditation" for executives. At 8 a.m. all directors sit with eyes closed, while the CFO quietly counts the budget on his fingers. Join in?
Your assistant notes you haven't taken leave in 14 months. By law and common sense, that's a lot. HR sent a warning. To you. The CEO. What now?
In the evening you find the guitar you played in college at the back of a closet. Dusty, out of tune, but yours. An hour till bed. Play or read a report?
Someone found out you play guitar. Now the office band wants you for the company party. Rehearsals Wednesdays at 7 p.m. Join?
The office band wants you to sing an original song called "Quarterly Report." An accountant wrote the lyrics, and they're bold. Sing it?
At the party your band performs. You forget the second verse and the whole room sings it for you. Turns out everyone knows the words. What next?
The sales director proposes a "gift" for an official who could speed up the new warehouse permit. He says "everyone does it." Your answer?
Marketing wants "natural product" on the package. Technically it's 51% true. Legal says "it's allowed." Your conscience says not really. Your decision?
An anonymous email arrives in the evening: the sales department's financial report is "slightly embellished." The quarter closes tomorrow. Check now?
The check shows the sales report was padded by 3%. The sales director calls it "an optimistic forecast." The board must be told. Who tells them?
A big client sent you an expensive watch "as a token of friendship." Company rules forbid gifts above a certain value. It's a beautiful watch. What do you do?
A childhood friend writes in the evening: his firm is bidding in your company's tender. He's not asking for anything, "just so you know." What do you do?
Your childhood friend's firm won the tender fair and square: best price. But the smokers' corner is whispering that "the CEO got his buddy in." What now?
HR wants to fire an employee who publicly criticized the company on social media. The criticism is, frankly, fair. Fire him?
The employee who criticized the company brings you a list of 12 improvements. Eight are sensible. He's expecting to be fired. What do you do?
left: Put him in charge of three
right: Thank him and let him go

text: At 8:30 a.m. a courier delivers a parcel marked "Into the CEO's hands only." Inside: a pie from the grandma of an employee you helped. Note: "Eat it yourself." Share it?
A courier is stuck in your elevator with the board documents. The board meets in 15 minutes. The elevator tech arrives in 40. What now?
Late in the evening you get stuck in an elevator with the cleaner. No signal. The next 30 minutes are the most honest of your career: she tells you how things really work. Listen?
You implemented three of the cleaner's ideas after the elevator. Now directors drop by her "for advice" before meeting you. She doesn't like it. What now?
You get a letter from a six-year-old customer: "Dear director, your toy broke but I still love it. Please fix it." Reply personally?
left: Reply and send a new one

text: A board member calls in the evening to say "some on the board" have doubts about your style. He won't say who. Or what. Find out?
The board chair suggests a weekly breakfast "to stay in sync." 6:30 a.m. at his favorite café across town. Agree?
At breakfast the board chair spends half an hour on his country house instead of syncing up. You learned more about rose varieties than strategy. Is this normal?
In the evening the board chair sends a photo of a rose: "Named a variety after the company." You need to reply. Your reply is practically a strategy statement.
The press secretary asks you not to wear your favorite bobble hat in public: "A CEO can't wear a pompom." It's minus twenty outside. Wear it?
Your bobble hat photo hit the news: "A Human CEO." Pompom hat sales in your city went up. Marketing is in shock. What now?
Friday evening, the weekly report arrives. All the numbers are good except one, which is bold and red. Open it now or Monday?
The building has a separate "executive" elevator. It's faster, but it's always just you and silence. The shared one has a queue and gossip. Which do you take?
Staff joke that you need an invitation to get onto the executive floor. HR suggests putting an open kitchen there for everyone. Do it?
Your new CEO chair broke on the first evening: the back reclines to horizontal without warning. The supplier promises a replacement in a month. What now?
The corridor has portraits of every past CEO. PR asks when you can sit for the painter. Twelve two-hour sessions. Agree?
The painter unveils your portrait. You look older, wiser, and somehow there's a dog you don't own. Hang it?
left: Hang it and adopt a dog
right: Ask him to paint out the dog

text: The board gives you a new company car. It's huge, black and doesn't fit in your building's parking. Neighbors ask "who moved in." Swap it?
right: Keep it, park round the corner

text: The day before the AGM, legal brings 60 "possible questions." Number 47: "Why does the CEO need such a big car?" What do you prepare?
At the AGM an elderly shareholder brings a notebook and reads out your promises from last year. Three of five weren't kept. He isn't angry, just reading. Your answer?
At the AGM shareholders vote on your pay package. "For" is at 51% and counting. The chair suggests trimming your bonus right now "just in case." Agree?
After the AGM you walk into the empty hall. 300 name badges on the chairs, and the forgotten notebook of that elderly shareholder. Return it personally?
The minority shareholders' association asks to meet: "Nobody listens to us, except maybe you." There are twelve of them, holding 0.3% together. Meet?
Your largest shareholder pitches you a new business line at a meeting. The idea is weak, but he's big. How do you respond?
right: Pilot it to avoid a fight

text: In the evening a shareholder writes to you directly, bypassing the board chair: "I want a new CFO. No fuss." What do you do?
The CFO found out the shareholder wants him out. He comes in at 7:30 with five years of reports: "Should I start packing?" Your answer?
At the board meeting you defend the CFO. The chair asks: "Will you stake your reputation on him?" All eyes on you. Will you?
After the board meeting the chair takes you aside: "Well done today. Just don't do it again." You're not sure that's praise. Ask what he means?
The board chair's aide calls at 7:10: "He'd like a short summary from you every morning. Five lines." One more daily task. Agree?
Every day, line five of your summary for the chair is "Everything's under control." Today it isn't. Tell the truth in the morning summary?
Your inner voice asks in the evening: "When did you last do something you like, not something you have to?" You remember the guitar. And the portrait with the dog. What now?
Security proposes a new access system: everyone goes through a scanner, you included. Morning queues of 15 minutes. Staff are unhappy. Introduce it?
Security found a bug on your desk. It turns out to be your kid's toy spy gadget, slipped into your briefcase. The board has already heard about "the incident." Explain?
Security reports someone was photographing your house. It turns out to be a photographer for an article: "Where CEOs Live." Sue?
left: Ask them to remove the photos

text: PR asks you to start a "CEO's Notes" blog for staff. Weekly, a thousand characters, "in a lively voice." Your lively voice is spreadsheets. Write it?
Your first "CEO's Notes" post, about being late to your own meeting because of the elevator, got more views than the annual report. Keep going?
Under a blog post an employee asks: "Does the CEO get tired?" You want to answer "very," but PR suggests "Energy is our strength." What do you write?
The strategy session opens with: "What will you stop doing next year?" All directors go quiet. Each fears it'll be their department. Set an example?
left: Name one of your own projects

text: At the session, the CFO and marketing director spend 50 minutes arguing over what "customer-centricity" means. The facilitator whispers: "Lunch, maybe?" Call a break?
The outcome of the two-day strategy session: 400 sticky notes on the wall. Your assistant asks what to do with them: photograph, transcribe or toss?
PR wants to film "A CEO's Morning": you wake, exercise, sip healthy tea. In reality you wake up and read email. Film the truth?
Shares rose 7% after the "CEO's Morning" video. You filmed it with a sore throat and mismatched socks. Analysts praise its "authenticity." Do it again?
In the evening social media is buzzing about your mismatched socks. A sock brand offers an ad deal. PR is at a loss. Your answer?
right: Ask for socks for the staff

text: Your phone rings at 5:50 a.m. An investor in another time zone "didn't think about the time." He wants to discuss one slide. Answer?
During an important bank call a courier bursts in with a huge box: "Your smart-office equipment!" You didn't order it. The CIO did. What now?
right: Put it in a shared meeting room

text: At 11 p.m. your smart speaker at home announces: "Reminder: breakfast with the board chair at 6:30 tomorrow." Nobody set it up. Your assistant did. Unplug it?
The first working morning of the year. Your assistant proposes a 30-item list of "CEO goals." Number one: "Work less." Number two: "Grow revenue 20%." Approve?
Marketing proposes renaming "Chief Executive Officer" to "Chief Inspiration Officer." It's trendy. The board objects. Staff are laughing. Your call?
You're the last to leave. The guard switches off the lights floor by floor. One desk lamp is on: an intern finishing a report for you. It's due Monday. What do you do?
HR wants you to personally pick 20 people for the "future leaders" pool. 600 candidates, 600 forms. Your assistant is bringing the first box.
The leadership pool includes the CFO's son and the sales director's nephew. Both look strongest on paper. But rumors have started. Keep them?
At the first future-leaders session, a young employee asks: "What scares you as CEO?" Twenty people wait for an honest answer. What do you say?
In the morning you find your office was "sanitized" overnight and everything rearranged. The desk now faces the wall. It feels like someone else's office. What now?
The guard at the gate says he's writing a book, "Thirty Years at the Gate." There's a chapter about you. He offers to let you read it. Read it?
The chapter in the guard's book is titled "The New CEO Who Says Hello." You read it in the evening and are unexpectedly moved. Offer to publish it at company expense?
You've been nominated for "CEO of the Year." Entry requires a 30-page form about your achievements, written in the third person. Enter?
PR rewrote your award entry. Now you're "a visionary who transformed the industry." The industry doesn't know that yet. Submit as is?
Award night. You didn't win; the rival CEO did. Cameras zoom in on your reaction. What do you do?
The morning after the ceremony, staff send you a homemade certificate: "Best CEO — according to our department." Signed by 40 people. Hang it?
A business school invites you to lecture executive students. Topic: "CEO Mistakes." Your list is long. Use them all?
After your lecture, a student asks for a job. He's the CEO of a small firm and ready to start in a junior role. Hire him?
A publisher offers you a book deal: "The Road to the Top." You'd have to write at night. PR is thrilled; your family less so. Agree?
The publisher sends the cover of your future book. You're standing on a mountaintop in a suit. You've never been on a mountain in a suit. Approve?
The publisher offers a ghostwriter to "write it in your voice." After chapter one you learn a lot about yourself. For instance, that you love fishing. Now what?
Comms is preparing your New Year video message to staff. The script: 4 minutes of good wishes and 11 minutes of yearly KPIs. Shorten it?
HR asks what to give staff for New Year: a calendar with your photo, or an extra day off. The CFO prefers the calendar; it's cheaper. Decision?
New Year party. The emcee announces a quiz: "Who knows the CEO best?" The winner knows more about you than your family does. Scary?
December 31, 9 a.m. The board sends "a small request": a quarterly forecast by January 2. You and the CFO have holiday plans. What do you do?
left: Do it yourself, spare the CFO
right: Ask for an extension to the 10th

text: It's your birthday. Your assistant reveals the whole office will "happen" to gather in the hall with a cake at lunch. You must look surprised. Can you pull it off?
Your birthday evening. 300 messages of congratulations. Replying to each takes two hours. Your family waits at home with cake number two. What now?
HR offers executives sessions with the company counselor. You don't think you need it. Your assistant quietly books you for Thursday. Go?
The counselor asks: "When did you last say 'no' without explaining?" You can't recall. She offers to let you practice on her. Try it?
In the evening the sales director asks you to speak at a client event on Saturday. You remember the counselor. Try a "no" with no explanation?
Saturday, 8 a.m. The CFO calls: "Sorry to bother you on a weekend. It's not about work. Actually, it is." Answer?
On Sunday at the playground another parent recognizes you and starts complaining about your product. Your kid is on the slide, watching. What now?
Sunday, 8 p.m. You know if you open email, Monday starts tonight. If you don't, the morning will be rough. Open it?
Monday, 7:45 a.m. Your assistant says "nothing happened" over the weekend, then adds: "Except three things." Those three things eat the whole morning. Delegate?
The CIO asks you to an "informal" lunch. He says he wants to leave and start his own company. In his shoes, you'd go too. What do you say?
right: Persuade him to stay a year

text: Your old mentor, a former CEO himself, calls in the evening: "How are you?" He's the only one who asks without an agenda. Be honest?
A procurement specialist writes to you: eight years in the same role, newcomers get promoted, she doesn't. Her manager is on vacation. Reply?
You learn she wasn't promoted because "the department would fall apart without her." A compliment turned into a trap. What do you do?
left: Promote her and find a backup

text: An evening email from a former employee, fired under your predecessor. He believes he was treated unfairly and asks only for an apology. Apologize on the company's behalf?
An investor fund asks you in the morning to name "the company's top three risks." You know five, but two are members of the board. What do you list?
Investor day. You're presenting to analysts, and someone in the front row is asleep. He's the analyst from the biggest bank. His forecast moves the stock. Wake him?
left: Crack a joke to wake him

text: In the evening the sleeping analyst publishes his note: "The presentation was soothingly stable." Rating: "Buy." Is that good?
A trade magazine named you one of the "40 Most Influential CEOs." The photo shoot is at a studio at 7 a.m., posing with three competitors. Go?
At the shoot the photographer lines up four CEOs shoulder to shoulder and asks them to "show industry unity." The rival to your right quietly steps on your foot. An accident?
Staff in the group chat in the evening: "The CEO's in a magazine as one of the most influential. Meanwhile our coffee machine has been broken for three days." Reply in the chat?
In the morning you personally show up on the floor with a new coffee machine. Staff applaud. The procurement director goes pale: it wasn't budgeted. What do you say?
right: Ask him to process it retroactively

text: The procurement director brings you the rules: even the CEO can't buy coffee machines without a tender. He's right. You're still a little hurt. What now?
In the evening the CFO shows you coffee spending rose 40%. Productivity rose 12%. He asks whether that's "good or bad." Your answer?
You're ten minutes late to your own meeting. Third time this week. The directors have started arriving ten minutes late too. What now?
left: Introduce a fine, pay it first
right: Move the start time by ten

text: The lateness fine: every latecomer drops a coin in a jar. After a month you've paid more than anyone. The jar is full. Where does the money go?
The meeting started at 6 p.m. and was scheduled for an hour. It's 8:30. Nobody leaves because you don't. And you don't because they don't. Who goes first?
Morning. The reception coffee machine is broken. You're offered tea. You haven't had tea in twenty years. First meeting in five minutes. Decide.
Renovation on the floor above: someone's drilling right over your office all afternoon. You have three video calls back to back. Ask them to stop?
right: Ask them to stop the works

text: 10:15 p.m. The last call of the day, with Asia. You're so tired that to "How are you?" you answer: "Quarterly." Pause. The partners wait. How do you recover?
7 a.m. Legal reports a big competitor is quietly buying your shares and already holds 9%. A takeover attempt is possible. The board doesn't know yet. First move?
The rival CEO calls you personally: "Let's keep it friendly. After the merger you'll stay — as a deputy." Very friendly tone. Your reply?
In the evening staff learn about the possible takeover from the news. Panic in the group chat: "Are we being sold?" They need your answer by morning. What do you write?
The banker proposes a takeover defense: find a friendly investor. The friendly investor wants two board seats and your promise to "listen." Agree?
You're calling major shareholders so they don't sell to the rival. Twelfth call. A shareholder asks: "What's in it for me?" Your answer?
The takeover attempt is repelled. The rival owns 14%, but no control. The directors want to celebrate. You haven't slept in three days. Celebrate?
The rival, now holding 14% of your shares, has the right to ask questions at the meeting. He sent 80. Answer them all?
Consultants propose cutting 12% of staff. The board agrees. You know costs could be cut another way, but it's slower. What do you do?
Three evenings with the CFO and a spreadsheet, and you've found a way to save without layoffs. It needs sacrifice at the top: executive pay minus 20%. Including yours. Agree?
You announce a 20% pay cut to the directors. Two agree at once, one says nothing, one says "it's not my problem." What do you do?
At the town hall you announce there'll be no layoffs; instead executives take a pay cut. Silence. Then someone starts clapping. Then everyone. What do you say next?
At home you announce your pay is dropping 20%. Your kid asks whether the beach trip is cancelled. You hadn't thought about that. Your answer?
Your first visit to a regional office. The branch director meets you at the station with an employee band. Out of tune, but trying very hard. What do you do?
At the regional office staff show you everything "just like at HQ." The kitchen has the same coffee machine — broken. The branch director says it's "just for show." What do you do?
right: Promise to include it in the budget

text: In the evening the branch director invites you home for dinner. His family has been cooking for three days. Your train back leaves in two hours. Go?
The overnight train back. Your compartment mate is an engineer from your own company on a business trip. He doesn't know who you are. Introduce yourself?
The engineer from the train only finds out who you are at the station. He goes pale: all night he was saying "the CEO knows nothing about production." What do you say?
The engineer from the train gives you an evening tour of production "as it really is." You learn more than from two years of reports. The plant director is nervous. What about him?
You decide to answer support calls in person once a month. The first customer shouts that his order is lost. You don't know how to use the system. What now?
left: Call an agent over to help

text: After a day on the support desk you realize agents work with an ancient system that was promised a replacement long ago. The CIO says "next year." Your response?
In the evening the agent you shadowed all day writes: "For once, a CEO knows how hard our job is." How do you reply?
Morning rumor: the CEO wants to move headquarters to another city. Not true. But the marketing director admits he "discussed it hypothetically." What now?
The board proposes you also take on the role of executive chairman. More power, more responsibility, even more meetings. Accept?
Your assistant asks whether to keep your Saturday "Fishing with Dad" slot. The board chair wants a call at that time. Which wins?
Fishing with your dad. He asks why you check your phone every five minutes if "the fish aren't biting anyway." Fair point. Put it away?
On the fishing trip your dad says: "I was a shift supervisor in my day. Know what matters? Feed people and let them go home." A 20-year strategy. Write it down?
left: Write it down and apply it

text: You bring a new idea to the meeting: "People should go home on time." Directors nod, but at 8 p.m. they're all still there. How do you make it stick?
right: Start by leaving on time yourself

text: You switched off email at 7 p.m. In the morning you find 40 people sent documents through personal messengers instead. Security is horrified. Roll it back?
You're having lunch with three random employees from different departments. One is silent the whole time, one never stops talking, the third asks about pensions. How do you steer it?
left: Give the quiet one the floor

text: A partner invites you to a restaurant where one dinner costs as much as your support agent's monthly salary. Declining is awkward. Going is awkward. Which?
Your office is now next to a room where sales holds "energetic" standups every morning with clapping and shouts of "Yes!" At 8:30. Ask them to tone it down?
right: Ask them to keep it down

text: A young employee proposes "meeting-free Fridays." Directors object: "When do we decide things?" Staff are for it. Introduce it?
The "meeting-free Friday" pilot is over. Productivity went up, but two directors held meetings "at the café, doesn't count." How do you react?
Your assistant noticed you skipped breakfast three days running and booked "Breakfast — mandatory" in your calendar. It can't be moved; it's marked red. Comply?
A courier from your own delivery service brings your lunch. He asks for a selfie: "My mom won't believe it." Investors are waiting in reception. Take it?
In the evening your kid draws your company for a school project: a big building, a tiny figure in a window. Caption: "This is where my CEO lives." What do you say?
The conference organizers slotted you first, at 9 a.m. on Saturday. The first speaker usually talks to an empty hall. Speak?
You're speaking to a hall with nine people. Three are your own staff who came to support you. Give the talk, or sit with them and chat?
11:30 p.m. You switch off your office light and see every window in the building is dark. Except yours. Security is waiting to lock up. You wanted to finish an email. Leave?
A film crew wants to shoot a documentary: "A Week in the Life of a CEO." The camera follows you everywhere except the bathroom. Possibly there too. Agree?
The documentary cameraman asks you to "walk into the meeting room again, more decisively." Seventh take. The directors inside are waiting for your decisive entrance. One more?
In the evening the director shows a rough cut. The film's highlight: you feeding pigeons outside the office and discussing the quarterly plan with them. Keep it?
The sales director, 15 years in, asks to leave: "I'm tired." He's the company's best seller. Without him the plan is at risk. What do you offer?
The board demands you fire the marketing director over a failed campaign. You approved the campaign. The board seems to have forgotten. Remind them?
In the evening the marketing director you defended brings you a book inscribed: "To the one who didn't throw me under the bus." You don't know where to look. What do you say?
