The headhunter sends three CFO candidates: one from a big corporation, one from a startup, and a former classmate you haven't spoken to in 15 years. Who first?
The CFO candidate asks: "Why did the last CFO leave?" The true answer takes 40 minutes and involves the word "fishing." How do you answer?
In the evening you choose between two finalists. One is easygoing and agrees with everything. The other is difficult and strong. The board recommends "easygoing." Who do you hire?
On day one the new CFO cancels your pet project: "It doesn't pay off." He's right. You hired him for exactly this. Still stings. What do you do?
HR proposes refreshed company values: "Speed, Synergy, Swagger." You notice they just all start with the same letter. Approve?
You asked staff to write the company values themselves. 400 responses. The most popular: "Don't lie, don't delay paychecks." Use it?
Eco activists stand at the entrance with a banner about your packaging. It really does have a lot of plastic. PR suggests leaving through the back. What do you do?
left: Go out and talk to them

text: After meeting the activists you propose switching to cardboard packaging. It costs 8% more. The CFO looks at you as if you'd suggested gold wrapping. Insist?
Staff propose a "car-free day": everyone comes by bike or public transport. Including the CEO. Support it?
Car-free day. You arrive by bike, soaked, suit crumpled. Bank meeting in 20 minutes. Staff are snapping photos and liking them. What now?
left: Go to the meeting as is

text: The banker eyes your soggy look and says: "Cutting costs, I see. Good sign for a lender." He smiles. You're not sure it's a joke. Play along?
In the evening someone hit "reply all" on a 3,000-person list. Within an hour, 200 "Remove me from this list" emails. Half from directors. Step in?
Your email to staff went out with a typo: instead of "Thanks for your hard work" it reads "Thanks for your hard word." The company's grammar fans are discussing. Correct it?
You're asked to sign 400 thank-you letters to staff. Your assistant suggests a signature stamp. You're on number 100 by hand. Your hand is tired. Keep going?
In the evening you discover there's only one company seal, in your safe. Only your assistant knows the code, and she's home. The document is due by midnight. Call her?
Veterans propose a company museum. It needs a room. The only free one is your private lounge. Give it up?
The veterans gathered exhibits for the museum. Among them: your old intern badge with an awful photo. It'll be the centerpiece. Agree?
In the evening you wonder what you'll leave behind at the company. So far: a museum with your badge, the eyebrow meme and a coffee machine. Add something serious?
right: Let the coffee machine be it

text: Staff ask to allow dogs in the office on Fridays. One dog already secretly lives in accounting. They hide it, but it barks at phone calls. Make it official?
During your video call with the board, the accounting dog runs into your office and sits right in frame. The chair goes silent. What do you do?
left: Introduce the dog to the board
right: Quickly shoo it out of frame

text: In the evening the board chair writes: "What's the dog's name? I have one just like it." His first personal message in a year. How do you reply?
left: Tell him all about the dog

text: The CIO gives you a smartwatch that shows your stress level. It's 8:20 a.m. and it already says "critical." Wear it?
left: Take it off and give it back

text: During a meeting your smartwatch buzzes and announces loudly: "Time for a breathing exercise." All the directors look at you. Do it?
In the evening the smartwatch sends a report: "You were calm for 11 minutes today." Those were 11 minutes in the elevator. Food for thought?
right: Take the watch off for good

text: The office has 30 meeting rooms, all named after rivers. The new marketing director wants to rename them after "company values." Staff are used to meeting "at the Volga." Your decision?
You arrive for a meeting in the "Ob" room, and another meeting is already on. The organizer is an intern. He doesn't recognize you and politely asks you to wait. Wait?
right: Ask him to clear the room

text: An evening call with partners. You forget to mute for ten minutes and tell your family what's for dinner. The partners listen attentively. What now?
left: Make a joke and carry on

text: Your assistant asks what goes first on the management board agenda: the supplier problem or the accountant's anniversary. 30 minutes total. Which first?
Your biggest client wants a clause: "The CEO personally answers the client's calls 24/7." It's a huge contract. Sign?
The client with the 24/7 clause calls at 11:40 p.m. to ask how you're doing. Just because. It's a test. Answer?
A delegation from analytics waits in reception. Not asking for raises, but for decent monitors. Two brought their old ones to show you. What do you do?
After the monitor story, five more departments show up: chairs, lamps, kettles, keyboards and "just everything." Your reception area turns into a warehouse. What now?
In the evening your personal number accidentally leaks into the company-wide chat. Within an hour, 70 employees have messaged you ideas. Some are good. Change your number?
The logistics director wants new courier uniforms: "Brighter, like the competitors'." The couriers want warmer, not brighter. Whose side?
You're trying on the new courier uniform to check if it's warm. Just then a delegation of investors walks in. You're in a logo beanie. What do you do?
In the evening the couriers send a photo: all in the new warm uniforms, out in the cold, thumbs up. Caption: "Thanks, boss." Forward it to the board?
Time to write the annual shareholder letter. Last year's opened with "It was a challenging year." So did the year before's. How do you start this time?
Legal struck every lively phrase from your shareholder letter. What's left: "The company continued to implement its strategy." Safe and lifeless. Fight for your phrases?
The CFO proposes a share buyback: "It'll support the stock." The money is what you wanted to invest in the new plant. Which?
Annual results day. The report goes out at 7 a.m. You've been up since 4:30 and reread it three times, though you know it by heart. Get up or try to sleep?
left: Get up and take a walk

text: The annual results are good, but the stock still fell 2% after publication. Analysts write: "Expected more." You expected less. What do you tell the team?
In the evening an old classmate writes: "Saw your results. Not bad for a C student." You were a C student. Reply?
The industry regulator asks you to explain the price rise. One week to respond. Legal wants your signature on every page. There are 60. Sign?
right: Sign the first and last only

text: A scheduled inspection arrives. The inspector asks for "a quiet office." The quietest is yours. Give it up?
At the end of the day the inspector says: "I've seen many companies. At least your people aren't afraid of the CEO." Best review of the year. Tell the team?
In the morning your spouse says he's been offered a promotion in another city. He asks what you think. Your company is here; his chance is there. Your answer?
You discuss a possible move with your family. Your kid says: "You're always at work anyway. What does it matter which city?" Fair and painful. What now?
In the evening you and your spouse decide: he takes the promotion remotely, and you promise two work-free evenings a week. The board doesn't know about the evenings. Keep the promise?
Your first agreed "work-free evening." At 6:30 p.m. the board chair wants "five urgent minutes." You're already home. Answer?
left: Let it ring, call back at dawn

text: Your kid needs help with a school project: "A model of your parent's workplace." You try to build the office out of cardboard and get a box with windows. The kid is happy. Are you?
Parents' evening. Your first in a year. The teacher asks: "And you are?" Other parents know you from the news. What do you say?
Morning in the airport business lounge. The rival CEO is at the next table. You both pretend not to recognize each other. This goes on for 40 minutes. Say hello?
On the plane your seatmate is the rival CEO. Six-hour flight. He opens a laptop with his strategy deck. The screen is perfectly visible. What do you do?
At the hotel in the evening you realize you forgot your charger. Phone at 3%. Tomorrow's 8 a.m. meeting — address and passwords — are all on the phone. What now?
6:30 a.m. in a strange city. You woke up and for a minute didn't know where you were. Then you did. Then you remembered: five meetings. There's a buffet, but only time for coffee. Which?
A client in another city shows you his plant, then invites you to the local team's match. You're not a fan. Three hours. Go?
At the stadium the client celebrates a goal by hugging you. The stadium camera shows you on the big screen. An hour later: local news photo, "CEO cheers for our team." What now?
Your flight back is delayed four hours. You see your luggage left without you. In it: your suit for tomorrow's board meeting. What now?
left: Buy a suit at the airport
right: Show up to the board in a sweater

text: You show up to the board meeting in a sweater. The chair looks surprised, then says: "Thank goodness, we can lose the ties." Everyone takes off their ties. What next?
In the evening your lost suitcase is delivered. Instead of your suit: someone else's things and a teddy bear with a note, "Don't forget to call Mom." Not yours. What do you do?
right: Hand it to lost and found

text: The teddy bear's note reminded you: you haven't called your mom in two weeks. It's 7:50 a.m., meeting in ten minutes. Mom gets up early. Call?
Mom asks what you had for lunch. You can't remember. Mom goes silent the way only moms can. Your answer?
Mom texts in the evening: "Saw you on TV. Are you even eating? Come over on Sunday." You have an investor call on Sunday. Go?
The CIO brings a five-year digital transformation plan. Budget: three years of profit. Slide 2 says "This is non-negotiable." Negotiate?
The CIO wants every employee, you included, to take a course on the new system. 16 hours. You could exempt yourself, but people would notice. Take it?
In the evening you take the exam for the new system. You score 62 out of 100. An intern from next door got 98. Results are public. What do you do?
left: Ask the intern to teach you

text: The intern who scored 98 gives you a lesson on the new system at 8 a.m. He's nervous and calls you "Comrade CEO." How do you break the ice?
left: Ask him to use your first name

text: The new accounting system is live. The very first transaction — your expense report — went to marketing instead of accounting. Marketing is shocked by your receipts. What now?
In the directors' chat someone sends a cat sticker. A minute later, another. Ten minutes later the whole chat is stickers. The budget discussion drowned. Join in?
You run an idea contest. Prize: a day as CEO. The winner is a forklift driver from the warehouse. He arrives at 7 a.m. in his best jacket. Hand him the chair?
In his first three hours as CEO, the forklift driver cancelled two pointless meetings and signed an order for new gloves for the warehouse. The directors are impressed. What about the order?
right: Revoke it — it was a game

text: In the evening the forklift driver hands back the chair: "Tough job you've got. But way too many meetings." You knew that. He said it out loud. What next?
right: Thank him and get back to work

text: At 8:15 a.m. you see couriers and stockers waiting in the cold for the staff door to open. The main entrance is open, but "office only." What do you do?
left: Open the main entrance to all
right: Ask someone to sort it out

text: The safety engineer asks you to complete a briefing before visiting the shop floor. 45 minutes. You've been there a hundred times. But rules are rules. Do it?
In the evening a photo of you on the shop floor with your hard hat on backwards lands in a trade publication: "Safety from the top." The safety engineer is furious. What now?
A note in the shared kitchen: "Whoever ate my yogurt — have you no shame?" Someone added below: "It was the CEO." You didn't eat it. Deny it?
The chief accountant asks: can your lunch with a client count as an entertainment expense if the client is "sort of a friend"? Your answer?
In the evening you notice the meeting room clocks all show different times. Up to 12 minutes apart. That explains half the year's late arrivals. Who takes charge?
left: You, for the fun of it

text: Your two deputies arrive at 7:45 with two different plans for the same project. Each is sure you're on their side, because yesterday you nodded at both. Did you?
right: Ask them to merge the plans

text: Your deputies compete to be first to answer your emails. The record is 14 seconds. You're writing at 11 p.m. and realize both will reply in the night. Send it?
One deputy writes in the evening: "If you pick his plan, I'm leaving." The other says nothing, but you know he's thinking the same. What now?
You put both deputies in charge of the project jointly. Two hours later, two separate project meetings appear in your calendar at the same time. Which do you attend?
left: Neither — let them sort it out

text: Your deputies unexpectedly made peace and come to you together: "Let's reduce your involvement in day-to-day operations." Sounds like care. Or a plot. Agree?
In the evening you realize for the first time in a year you could skip a meeting and nothing would break. That's both pleasing and scary. What do you do with the time?
Your IR head suggests asking shareholders what they want from the CEO. Top answer: "Predictability." You've just announced a surprising strategy. What now?
left: Explain the logic in a letter

text: A major shareholder invites you onto his yacht for an "informal chat about the future." Three other CEOs from his portfolio will be there. Sail?
Evening on the yacht. All four CEOs are seasick and dreaming of shore. The shareholder is having the time of his life. What do you do?
In the morning the yacht shareholder sends a photo: four CEOs on deck, all green. Caption: "Dream team." PR asks you not to share it. What do you do?
right: Forward it to the other three

text: The three CEOs from the yacht suggest a group chat: "Yacht Survivors." They're the first people you can talk to honestly about the job. Join?
At 11 p.m. the "Yacht Survivors" chat is discussing how to push back when the board is wrong. You type a long reply. Too candid?
A morning phone interview. The reporter asks about rumors of your resignation. You hadn't heard any. Now you have. Your answer?
PR finds out the resignation rumor started because you ordered business cards without your title. Just a printer's error. What now?
In the evening your kid asks: "Are you getting fired? Someone at school said so." The rumors reached the school. You feel very strange. Your answer?
You're invited to a live TV debate with the rival CEO. Topic: "Who really cares about customers?" Prepare?
During the debate the rival CEO pulls out your product and shows it's broken. You can see it's a counterfeit. Cameras are rolling. How do you react?
After the debate the rival CEO finds you backstage: "Sorry, they told me it was yours." He seems genuinely embarrassed. Accept the apology?
PR proposes a rule: no more than two interviews a month. This month you've already given five. What do you do?
The foundation the company has funded for five years is caught in a scandal: its director spent money on personal things. Journalists want your position. Your answer?
In the evening a foundation volunteer writes: "The director is gone, but the kids are still here. Please don't abandon them." The board advises distancing. What do you do?
Staff propose a volunteer day on the last Friday of each month. Directors fear missed deadlines. Staff fear you'll say no. Your decision?
Volunteer day. You're painting a kindergarten fence with the accountants. They paint perfectly straight; you don't. They politely repaint behind you. What do you do?
In the evening the kindergarten sends a photo of the fence: "Thanks to your company. Especially whoever painted the crooked bit — the kids love it." Hang it in the office?
You arrive at the warehouse at 5 a.m., end of the night shift, unannounced. The crew is drinking tea and arguing about football. Seeing you, everyone goes quiet. What do you say?
The night shift tells you there's no hot food: the canteen closes at 6 p.m. A fix is cheap. The CFO will likely object on principle. What do you do?
right: Ask the CFO to look into it

text: The first evening the night shift gets a hot meal. They send a photo: twenty people with bowls of soup, captioned "Dinner with the CEO." You're not there. What do you do?
The company veterans' council invites you to tea. Sixty retirees. Each wants to tell you how things used to be. 9 a.m. start, board meeting at 10:30. Go?
A veteran who worked at the plant for 40 years gives you a screwdriver: "This assembled the first batch." You don't know what to do with it, but you know it matters. Where does it go?
In the evening you notice you twirl the veteran's screwdriver during every hard call. It's calming. On video, the board chair asks what it is. Explain?
Your assistant suggests a separate "Write to the CEO" address for staff. No filters. No censorship. You'd read it yourself. Set it up?
left: Set it up and read it

text: In week one the "Write to the CEO" inbox got 600 emails. 200 complaints, 300 ideas, 100 plain thank-yous. You've been answering for three days. What next?
One evening email: "I've worked here for 3 years. Today for the first time I felt heard. Not asking for anything, just thanks." You sit and stare at the screen. Reply?
The company is moving offices. The designers gave you a glass-walled office "as a symbol of transparency." Everyone will see you all the time. Agree?
You've got used to working on display in the glass office. One day you nod off at your desk for ten minutes. You wake up to find someone has stuck a "Do not disturb" sign on the glass. What now?
The last evening in the old office. In a desk drawer you find a note from your predecessor: "Hang in there. The hardest part isn't the decisions, it's the loneliness." What do you do with it?
In the morning it strikes you: there's no one in the company you can say "I don't know" to. The CFO? Your assistant? The board chair? Try it?
At the directors' meeting you say: "I don't know how to solve this. Let's figure it out together." A pause. Then the directors start pitching ideas — the best all year. Keep doing this?
July, 34°C. The office AC can't cope. Facilities proposes allowing shorts. The sales director is horrified: "Clients will see!" Allow it?
Because of the heat you hold the directors' meeting in the park outside. The CFO brought a folding chair, the CIO an extension cord. The pigeons are interested in the budget. Carry on?
In the evening it's 38°C in the warehouse. Night-shift workers ask to cut the shift by an hour. The shipping plan is on fire. Your decision?
A meter of snow fell overnight. Half the staff can't get to the office. HR asks: declare a remote day? The board expects a report by noon.
You're stuck in the car on a snowed-in road. Board call in 40 minutes. The driver gets out a shovel. Help him dig, or prepare for the call?
In the evening, twenty people are stuck at the office because of the snow. Someone suggests ordering pizza and watching a movie in the meeting room. Stay with them?
HR is hosting a company sports day. You're asked to run the relay with the accounting team. Accounting has trained for a month. You haven't. Run?
left: Run and try not to let them down

text: In the relay you drop the baton. Accounting loses to sales. The chief accountant looks at you the way she looks at errors in a report. What now?
Accounting demands a rematch. Training is Tuesday and Thursday evenings — your "work-free evenings" promised to your family. Which do you pick?
Staff organized a chess tournament. In round one you draw a courier who turns out to be a near-master. Twelve minutes in, you're losing. Your reaction?
Facilities wants to remove all live plants from the office: "Nobody waters them." Staff launch a vote to save the ficuses. Who wins?
In the evening you notice the ficus in your office has dried up. Your assistant tactfully reminds you it was a gift from the board. What now?
Directors submit next year's budgets. Each asked for 30% more "so there's something to cut." You know this game. Your response?
You need to sign off on the directors' bonus system. The CFO proposes 40 KPIs. HR proposes 3. The directors want "simple and generous." How many KPIs?
In the evening you look at your annual goals set by the board. One is "increase employee engagement by 15%." You don't know how to measure it. What now?
Sales wants a 10% price rise from Monday. Marketing asks to wait until after the holidays. The CFO wanted it yesterday. Everyone's waiting on you. Decision?
After the price rise a loyal customer writes to you personally: "I've bought from you for 20 years. Explain why it's more expensive now." Reply yourself?
The sales director asks in the evening to give a big client a 30% discount "just this once." It's the fifth "just this once" this year. Allow it?
7:20 a.m. The CIO calls: the whole sales system is down. Cause: "an update nobody approved." Who approved it can be found out later. What now?
The system has been down for three hours. Stores are recording sales in notebooks. The board wants a report every 15 minutes. You're writing reports instead of helping. What now?
By evening the system is back. The culprit: an intern who wanted to "just update an icon." The CIO wants him fired. Your call?
The intern who crashed the system comes to you at 8 a.m. with a four-page written explanation and a cake. Clearly baked overnight out of nerves. How do you receive him?
left: Thank him and eat the cake

text: A key supplier reports a delay: a ship with components is stuck in port for a month. Production stops in two weeks. Procurement suggests air freight. Three times the cost.
In the evening the logistics director proposes no longer keeping "just in case" stock to save money. Yesterday, "just in case" stock saved you. Your answer?
The rival CEO calls early: his ship is stuck too. He proposes swapping components while the port is closed. Legal is nervous. What now?
The board learns about your parts swap with the rival and asks whether you're "getting too friendly." The swap saved production at both companies. Your answer?
In the evening the union brings its demand: a 12% wage increase. The CFO says 6% is possible. The union says 6% is an insult. How do you negotiate?
Eight hours into union talks. You've offered 9%, the union wants 10%. The union chair is an old classmate. He suggests settling "as friends." How?
Signing the collective agreement. The union chair asks for a group photo. In it you both look like people who haven't slept for two days. Publish it?
In the evening you count: you made 140 decisions this week. You remember six. The rest apparently made themselves. Worrying?
The young CEO of a small company asks you to mentor him. Monthly meetings, early, before work. You need a mentor yourself. Agree?
The young CEO asks: "How do you know when it's time to leave?" You've never thought about it. Now you are. Your answer?
In the evening your mentee sends his strategy and asks you to "take a quick look." 90 slides. He flies to investors in the morning. Help?
Staff propose a library in the lobby: everyone brings a book. You bring one on leadership. A week later nobody's borrowed it, while the accountant's detective novel has a waiting list. What now?
You convene a customer council. Ten top clients share what drives them nuts. By the fifth you realize it's all the same thing: your delivery service. What do you do?
right: Note it and discuss with the team

text: In the evening the logistics director is upset: "Clients complain, and you didn't defend us." He's right, you stayed silent. But the clients are right too. How do you talk to him?
left: Admit it, build a plan together
right: Tell him the client is right

text: Monday, 8 a.m. Six resignation letters from the marketing department in your inbox. All since the new director arrived. He doesn't know yet. What now?
At your talk, the new marketing director says: "They don't want to change." Those leaving say: "He won't listen." You've heard both lines before. What do you do?
In the evening three of the six leaving marketers agree to stay if they get a weekly meeting with you. Three more meetings a week. Agree?
A courier set a record: 64 deliveries in a day. The logistics director wants to hold him up as an example and raise everyone's target. Couriers object. Your decision?
The record-setting courier admits he did it because he's saving for his wedding. He's exhausted and doesn't want to repeat it. The logistics director is preparing a poster. What now?
In the morning a video appears online of "you" announcing a free product giveaway. The voice and face match; only the tie isn't yours. Customers are calling. What now?
left: Record a denial wearing that tie
right: Let legal handle it, stay quiet

text: Customers who came for the "free giveaway" are lining up outside stores. The sales director suggests handing out something "so they don't get angry." Do it?
A journalist digs up a 12-year-old post of yours: "All bosses are slackers." Now you're the boss of all bosses. Comment?
Your salary leaked online. It's 40 times the company average. In the staff chat they're calculating how many coffee machines it could buy. What now?
A business paper offers you a monthly column. PR offers to ghostwrite it. Your name will be on it. Who writes it?
Your first column is out. Commenters argue about whether you wrote it. Your old school literature teacher writes: "I recognize the style. The commas are still all over the place." Reply?
right: Hand the column to an editor

text: You're on a live call-in radio show. The first caller is your own kid, asking when you'll be home. What do you say?
Young marketers want you to record short social videos: 15 seconds, trends, dances. You can't dance. But the reach is huge. Try it?
Your 15-second video, where you try to explain the quarterly report in 15 seconds and run out of time, hits a million views. Staff want a sequel. Film it?
HR proposes scholarships for employees' children. A small budget, but the board might ask "why." Set it up?
left: Set it up, explain to the board

text: At the scholarship ceremony a stockkeeper's daughter gives a speech: "I want to be a CEO like you. But sleep more." The room laughs. So do you. Your reply?
right: "I'll teach you how not to sleep"

text: Staff invite you to plant trees on Saturday. Everyone plants one with a name tag. PR wants your tree to be the biggest. What do you do?
Staff are raising money to fix the playground by the office. Your contribution will be visible. Too small: "stingy." Too big: "showing off." How much?
You promised to match every ruble staff donate to charity. They raised five times the usual. The matching budget's gone. What now?
left: Top it up from your own pocket

text: An evening letter from an elderly woman: your company's money renovated the care home where she lives. She sent hand-knitted socks. Mismatched. Wear them?
Your assistant says she declined 140 meeting requests this week. Among them: 12 from employees, 40 from vendors and one from your aunt. Review them?
left: Accept the staff and your aunt

text: Your assistant admits she dreams of becoming a project manager. She's the best assistant you've ever had. Let her go and you'll drown in your calendar again. What do you do?
right: Ask her to wait a year

text: In the evening your assistant leaves you a "What to do if I'm not here" list: 64 items. #1: "Don't agree to 6:30 breakfasts." #64: "Take care of yourself." What do you do?
right: Pass it to the next assistant

text: The calendar offers "smart scheduling": it finds meeting slots by itself. Overnight it found time for 11 meetings — over all your lunches until month-end. Turn it off?
To see everyone, you introduce 5-minute meetings. The CIO only manages to open his laptop. The sales director manages to ask for a discount. Keep the format?
You block "focus time" from 4 to 6 p.m. Within a week it's been taken by: the CFO, the board chair and an "urgent fire drill." Defend at least one day?
One year since the IPO. The bank that ran it invites you to "celebrate" at their office. Forty minutes of speeches about how wonderful it all is. The stock is up 3% in a year. Go?
An investor who bought at the IPO writes to you personally: "I put my retirement savings in. You promised growth." The stock is up 3%. Reply?
In the evening your IR head proposes an "open day" for retail investors. 500 people will come. Each will want a photo with you. Do it?
Open day. A retired retail investor asks you to personally show him around the plant. The other 499 are watching. You're running late for the next agenda item. What do you do?
The retired investor on the tour turns out to be an engineer who built the plant 40 years ago. He shows you spots where "it used to be better." Listen?
In the evening the retired engineer sends you 30 handwritten pages of plant modernization proposals, with drawings. Five ideas are brilliant. What do you do?
Your assistant whispers there's a betting pool on how long you'll last. The average bet: three years. You're one year in. What do you do?
HR wants to ban the betting pool as "unprofessional." You've already placed a bet. And it's winning. Ban it?
In the evening you accidentally send the directors' chat a message meant for your spouse: "Buy bread and don't forget I love you." Silence. Then the CFO reacts with a heart. What now?
In the morning the parking guard notices your car has a flat tire. He offers to pump it up himself. You're late for the board. Accept?
The management board secretary asks you to review the minutes. They say: "The CEO proposed giving it some thought." You proposed "acting immediately." Correct it?
In the evening the board chair calls: "Are you happy in this job?" It's the first time anyone's asked. Answer honestly?
Sales proposes giving clients your autographed book for the holidays. The book isn't written yet. The publisher expects the manuscript in three months. Agree?
The banker explains his bank is moving to an "agile model." He shows a diagram with 40 boxes. You came to discuss a loan. How do you steer back?
At home you sit on the couch and realize you don't know how to turn on the TV. New remote. Your kid explains it to you "like an intern." Listen?
HR proposes a "shadow board" of employees under 30. They'd discuss the same issues as the real board and give you their own recommendations. Set it up?
The shadow board unanimously votes against a project the real board already approved. Their arguments are stronger. The chair asks "who are these kids." Your answer?
An intern from the shadow board becomes your "reverse mentor," teaching you new tech. First assignment: figure out why your inbox weighs 40 gigabytes. Dig in?
right: Ask IT to clean it up

text: The board runs your annual performance review. You get a self-assessment form: "Rate your strategic vision from 1 to 10." What do you put?
The chair reads out your review: "A strong leader, but spends too much time on people." You're not sure that's a flaw. Push back?
In the evening legal brings a draft three-year renewal of your contract. It includes: "The CEO is available 24 hours a day." Sign?
The board offers to add a large severance payout to your contract. Staff got a 9% raise this year. If this gets out, it'll be awkward. Accept?
The compensation committee asks you to step out while they discuss your pay. You sit in the corridor for 50 minutes. Employees walk past, nodding sympathetically. Wait?
In the evening the board chair asks: "Who do you see in your seat in five years?" "Myself" sounds arrogant; "him" sounds risky. Your answer?
The COO asks to rename his title to "President." He likes the sound of it. It worries you a bit. Agree?
The CFO wants a board seat. "For efficiency." You can tell he wants to be closer to the shareholders than to you. Support him?
In the evening you notice three of your directors enrolled in the same "CEO Readiness" program. The company paid. You approved it. Worried?
The board hired an outside consultant to "observe your management style." He'll sit in on all your meetings for a week, silently taking notes. How do you behave?
On day three the observer can't help himself and interrupts your meeting: "Sorry, but you've interrupted the CFO three times." The directors freeze. What now?
The consultant's report arrives in the evening. Key finding: "The CEO does the work of three and can't delegate." You're reading it at 11:40 p.m. in the office. Get the irony?
You delegate AGM prep to your deputy. He sends you a plan for approval every two hours. Six plans in one day. Is this delegating?
The deputy you delegated to made a decision you disagree with. Not a disaster, just not what you'd choose. Overrule it?
The AGM went fine without you doing the prep. Better than usual, even. In the evening you feel both relief and jealousy. What now?
The rival CEO has resigned. His career ended after an interview where he said too much. A journalist calls you for comment. Comment?
The former rival CEO asks to meet. He wants a job. Any job. He's strong, but your directors fear he'll "bring his culture." Meet him?
Over tea in the evening, the ex-rival CEO tells you how hard his last year was. You recognize yourself in his story. Offer him an adviser role?
Traffic jam. You've been sitting for 50 minutes. The meeting starts without you. The driver suggests walking 15 minutes to the subway. It's raining. Walk?
You arrive at the meeting soaked. HR hands you a towel, the CFO hot tea, the CIO a charger. You feel warm in every sense. Say something?
In the evening you feel a cold coming on. Tomorrow at 9 there's an investor call. You could hand it to the CFO, or croak through it yourself. Which?
You're off sick. At 8 a.m. your assistant writes: "You're not working. I'm telling everyone you're busy with something important." Directors have sent 14 "urgent" emails. Open them?
On the second sick day you realize the company is running fine. Everything's on track. Nobody calls. Pleased or worried?
In the evening your driver calls: "How are you feeling? The car misses you." The only non-work call all day. You're touched. Your reply?
You return after being sick. Reception greets you with a balloon: "Get well, boss!" It's tied to your chair. Keep it?
right: Remove it before the bank meeting

text: The banker notices the "Get well" balloon behind you and asks about your health longer than about the loan. Bonding or risk assessment?
Evening. Your family declares a "dinner without the word 'work.'" Each mention means doing the dishes. You're on your third round of dishes. A signal?
Saturday, 10 a.m. You drop by the office to pick up papers and find seven employees working "on their own initiative." Praise them or send them home?
You find out the seven work weekends because their manager "asks them to be reachable." The manager is your favorite director. What do you do?
Your favorite director says in the evening: "I work weekends too. I thought you liked it." You realize this started with you. What do you say?
You start a tradition: every Monday at 9 you tell the directors how you spent your weekend. Work-free. First Monday. You've got nothing to tell. Now what?
HR shows data: employees who see the CEO often are less likely to quit. She suggests you walk one floor every day. Agree?
On your evening walk you find an employee asleep on the lounge sofa. He explains he lives far away and is waiting for the night train. What do you do?
At 7:40 a.m. you find the security guard reading your leadership book. He says: "Not bad, but you're kinder in real life." How do you react?
Friday planning meeting. Everyone proposes postponing the decision to Monday. You realize this has happened every Friday for a year. Break the cycle?
Friday, 6 p.m. You finished work on time. First time in a month. The office is still full, everyone watching to see if you leave. Do you?
Your assistant travels with you for the first time. She packed three chargers, a first-aid kit, a spare tie and a "disaster folder." You laugh — until you need the tie. What do you say?
On the trip your assistant sees you negotiate for the first time. Afterward she says: "Now I see why you're so tired." Your reply?
On the trip your assistant asks if she can visit the local museum instead of the partners' dinner. Without her you'll mix up names. Let her go?
left: Let her go to the museum
right: Ask her to come to dinner

text: A credit rating agency wants a meeting with the CEO: they're deciding whether to downgrade the company. Their analyst loves long answers. You have an hour. How do you prepare?
The rating analyst asks: "What will you do if everything goes wrong?" You have a plan B, but you don't like it yourself. Show it?
In the evening the agency keeps the rating, but with a "negative outlook." The CFO calls it "almost a win." The board calls it "almost a loss." How do you frame it for the team?
An international ESG rating gave the company a "C." Fund investors write: at "B" they'd buy more shares. "B" requires a 200-page report and new treatment facilities. Start?
A proxy adviser recommends shareholders vote against your pay plan: "Too complex." You don't fully understand it yourself. What now?
A foreign business paper asks for an interview. The journalist says it's about "the future of the industry." Your English is fine for deals, not for metaphors. Agree?
Your kid's school newspaper asks for an interview: "Job: Director." Seven questions. The first: "Do you ever cry at work?" Answer honestly?
You're invited onto an evening talk show. Topic: "Rich and Tired." PR thinks it's a chance to show your human side. You think it's a trap. Go?
On the talk show the host asks how much your suit cost. The audience is people in ordinary jobs. You don't know the price: it was a gift. What do you say?
left: "A gift, no idea of the price"

text: An employee posts a video of himself spending 40 minutes looking for a free meeting room. Half a million views, captioned "Heroes work here." How do you react?
A well-known actor posts that your product is "as dull as a meeting." He has ten million followers. Marketing is panicking. Respond?
The actor accepts and attends your meeting. An hour in he says: "I take it back. This is more exciting than the movies." The video's already online. What next?
There's flooding in the region of your plant. Plant workers are affected themselves but still come in. The plant director asks what to do. Your call?
left: Shut the plant for a week

text: The company sends aid to the flood zone. PR wants a big logo on every box. Volunteers say that looks odd. Logo?
In the evening you arrive in the flood zone. PR wants a photo of you in rubber boots. Locals want you to help load sandbags. Which?
The local kids' football team asks you to sponsor their kits. Marketing says it's "off-target." The kids sent a drawing of you as their goalkeeper. Help?
The kids' team invites you to play goalkeeper in a friendly. You let in seven goals. The kids are thrilled. The coach asks you to come back. Go?
The city museum asks the company to sponsor an exhibition on industrial history. Your plant is one of the exhibits. In return they offer a hall in your name. Agree?
left: Name the hall after the workers

text: A cleaner who's worked at the company for 20 years invites you to her daughter's wedding. Saturday, 2 p.m. Nothing's booked, but you planned to sleep in. Go?
At the wedding you're seated in the place of honor next to the bride's parents. The emcee announces: "A word from the CEO!" No speech prepared. What do you say?
By the next evening the whole company knows you went to the cleaner's daughter's wedding. The sales director asks: "Will you come to mine?" He's not getting married. Your reply?
Your assistant added a "7-minute buffer" between all your meetings. Directors think it's "their time" and book into the buffers. What now?
Someone peeked at your calendar and posted it in the company chat: "How the CEO lives." It shows "Break: restroom 3 min." Staff are delighted. What now?
In the evening you realize your solo slot "Think about strategy" has been moved 22 times. Your assistant asks whether to move it a 23rd time. Your answer?
You try a new morning ritual: 10 minutes of silence before the first email. At minute four the board chair calls. A test of the ritual or coincidence?
Your assistant booked you lunch at 12:30. At 12:28 you're in a "five-minute" meeting now 40 minutes long. The restaurant holds tables for 15 minutes. Which?
Your assistant suggests blocking "nothing" every Saturday. You agree. The first Saturday the board chair sees "nothing" and asks if he can have it. Your answer?
In the morning, for the first time in a year, you use your own product like a regular customer. Ten minutes in you understand why customers complain. Call the team?
The product team defends itself: "We did what your directors said." The directors say: "We followed your vision." Your vision was one slide two years ago. What now?
In the evening the product team asks you to be "chief tester" for the new version. Thirty minutes every evening. Another half hour of work. Agree?
You visit the company lab for the first time. The engineers show you a prototype and ask if you like it. You don't. You can see they've worked on it for six months. What do you say?
The lead engineer admits his idea has sat in a drawer for five years because "it never got past management." It looks interesting. Give him resources?
left: Give him a team and budget
right: Send it through the usual process

text: In the evening the head of product is upset: "You went around me and gave the engineer resources directly." You did. How do you fix it?
right: Explain it had to be done

text: In the company chat someone writes: "Does anyone know if the CEO works weekends? Always online." You are online. Right now. Reply?
You decide to turn off your "online" status for good. An hour later the sales director writes: "Are you okay? You're not online!" What now?
For the first time you leave your work phone at the office for the weekend. On Friday night you dream it's ringing. You wake at 3 a.m. Go get it?
Monday after a phone-free weekend. The company's still there. 14 missed calls, all solved without you. Your assistant is smiling. What does this tell you?
You're handed a dismissal order for a warehouse worker who keeps being late. He's late because he drives his child across town. Sign it?
In the evening the warehouse director writes that after the flexible-hours case, 30 more workers filed the same request. The warehouse runs on shifts. What do you do?
You launch "Coffee with the CEO": every week a random employee has coffee with you. The first name drawn is the CFO. He laughs: "We have coffee every day anyway." Redraw?
A young procurement specialist comes to "Coffee with the CEO." She's silent for 10 minutes, then: "Can I tell you the truth about procurement?" Listen?
In the evening you verify what she said. It's all true: purchases go through three unnecessary approvals. The procurement director is an old friend of the CFO. How do you act?
The agency unveils the new company logo. It cost a department's annual salary, and it's the old logo tilted 7 degrees. Approve?
right: Keep the old one for free

text: The marketing director proposes a company anthem. He wrote the words, his nephew the music. It'll be performed at the AGM. You've listened. Your verdict?
Marketing ordered 5,000 logo hoodies. The back says "The CEO is proud of you" with your signature. They've arrived. Hand them out?
The annual report designers want your photo against a sunrise on the cover. You ask for employee photos. Designers say: "Investors want to see the leader." Whose version?
The CFO shows that one division has lost money for three years. Closing it: 200 jobs. Keeping it: another year of losses. The board awaits your decision. What do you do?
left: Give it a year to turn around

text: In the evening the head of the loss-making division sends a three-page rescue plan. Simple, honest, with errors in the numbers. But there's life in it. What do you do?
The competitor cut prices 20%. The sales director demands you match it "by lunch today." The CFO says it'll kill margins. Your decision?
A big tech company proposes a partnership: their platform, your customers. The contract says: "The partner may use customer data." Sign?
In the evening your daughter asks why your company doesn't make "something for teens." She pitches the idea in five minutes. It's decent. Pass it to the product team?
"Bring Your Kids Day." The accountant's six-year-old sits in your chair and refuses to get up: "Now I'm the director." What do you do?
The six-year-old "director" issues three orders in an hour: ice cream for all, meetings no longer than a cartoon, and a nap after lunch for the director. Sign them?
Your mom visits and asks to see the office. In reception she tells your assistant stories from your childhood. Your assistant is taking notes. Stop her?
right: Whisk Mom off on a tour

text: After her visit Mom calls: "Nice office. But why do you look so pale?" and sends a soup recipe. How do you respond?
left: Make the soup on the weekend

text: The board suggests you polish your English for negotiations. The tutor can only come at 7 a.m. Three times a week. Agree?
right: Use an app in the car

text: Staff started a book club and invited you. This month: an 800-page novel. Meeting in two weeks. You only read reports. Join?
left: Join and read on the road

text: The office opened a gym. You signed up but never made it. The trainer left a note: "I believe in you. But your pass expires soon." Go today?
right: Give the pass to an intern

text: At the gym the CFO is on the next treadmill. He runs faster than you while briefing you on the budget. You're out of breath. What now?
You've decided to be in bed by 11. At 10:55 an email arrives: "Urgent, but morning is fine." Open it or go to sleep?
The board proposes holding a session at your plant. The plant director is terrified: three days to paint everything that doesn't move. Tell him "don't paint"?
During the site visit a board member steps in fresh paint. The plant director goes pale. The board member laughs: "Well, at least something's new." How do you lighten the mood?
In the evening board members ask to dine in the plant canteen. The cooks panic. Menu: meatballs and fruit punch. The board is delighted. What do you do?
A university asks you to take 30 summer interns. Directors call it "workload with no payoff." You were once an intern here yourself. Take them?
The interns ask to meet you. First question: "How did you become CEO?" The answer is long, with luck, mistakes and one disastrous office party. Tell all?
In the evening an intern writes: "Thanks for the talk. I've decided to become a director. Not a CEO — a school principal." Reply?
You arrive at a meeting and the room is empty. Your assistant explains: yesterday you said "cancel it," meaning a different meeting. The directors went off to work. Is this good?
Your assistant says last week you promised 11 people you'd "look into their issue." You did for two. Nine are waiting. What do you do?
right: Honestly say you can't get to it

text: You decide to stop saying "I'll take a look." In the evening the CIO asks you to approve a project. You open your mouth to say "I'll take a look." What do you say instead?
At the offsite the facilitator asks everyone to write a letter to the company from 2035. The CFO writes "We survived," the CIO "Robots replaced us." What do you write?
At the brainstorm the best idea comes from an assistant who came in to bring coffee. The directors smile politely and move on. You can see it's the best one. What do you do?
In the evening after the offsite you try to explain the new strategy to your driver. He listens and asks: "Will it raise people's pay?" Good question. Your answer?
8:10 a.m. The guard says three people are waiting outside your office: a courier, the lawyer and the CFO. All "urgent." Who goes first?
Legal reports: a supplier is suing over a typo. The contract says "30 years" instead of "30 days." The supplier wants payments for 30 years. What now?
In the evening you find out the contract typo was made by a lawyer who's now asking for a promotion. He doesn't know yet. Tell him before or after deciding?
In the morning you put on a jacket and find a note in the pocket from yourself six months ago: "Don't forget to rest." You never did. What do you do with it?
You took Friday off. At 11 a.m. you find yourself in the café across from the office with your laptop. Staff wave at you from the window. What now?
In the evening you decide to start a hobby unrelated to work. You pick pottery. In your first class the cup comes out shaped like a sales chart. A sign?
right: Gift the cup to the CFO

text: Your assistant asks what to give key partners for the holidays: expensive pens, or honey from the apiary where the chief engineer's son works. Which?
A partner who got the honey calls: "Best gift in 20 years. Where'd you get it?" He wants to order honey for his whole company. The engineer's son will be thrilled. Share the contact?
Late evening, an unknown number. It's the chief engineer's son: "Thanks, they ordered a whole year's harvest. Want a beehive as a gift?" A beehive?
left: Take it to your country house

text: In the morning your assistant puts two documents on your desk: the leave request you forgot to sign for yourself, and the one you forgot to sign for her. Which first?
A major shareholder wants you to speak at his private conference for other investors. Unpaid. Three hours' drive each way. Go?
On the drive back from the conference your driver plays music from your youth. You ride in silence for 40 minutes. The best 40 minutes of the week. Ask him to make it a habit?
Shareholders nominate a blogger who has criticized your company to the board. He has the minority votes. He could win. Meet him before the vote?
The blogger made it onto the board. At his first meeting he livestreams "from the lair." The chair is furious. Legal says it can't be banned. What do you do?
In the evening 200,000 people have watched the board meeting stream. Top comment: "The CEO was the only one talking sense." Shares went up. What next?
right: Ask him not to stream again

text: The investment committee is reviewing new equipment. Operations says "we need it," the CFO says "not now," and you remember promising the board "savings." Decision?
The external auditor found a 0.3% error in the accounts. Not fraud, just a mistake. But it must be disclosed publicly. The CFO asks for "something quiet." What do you do?
In the evening the auditor asks you to sign a letter that you "bear personal responsibility for the accuracy of the accounts." You reread "personal" five times. Sign?
The board chair asks to move your weekly meeting to 7 a.m., because "morning is the time of clarity." You agree about clarity, not about 7:00. Agree?
The board chair announces his retirement. Two candidates for his seat: one likes you, the other doesn't. The board votes. Get involved?
The board chair's farewell dinner. He takes you aside: "I was always tougher on you than on the others. Because you were worth it." What do you say?
left: "Thank you. I needed to hear that"

text: On day one the new board chair sends you 40 "getting to know you" questions. #1: "Why isn't the company in three markets yet?" #40: "How do you sleep?" Answer them all?
The new chair wants reports weekly instead of monthly. Your directors are already groaning. He says it's "more transparent." Agree?
In the evening the directors come to you together: weekly reports eat a day a week each. They ask you to shield them from the new chair. What do you do?
right: Ask them to bear with it

text: Your assistant suggests sending the chair one page of "Friday numbers" instead of weekly reports. Less work for directors, same transparency for him. Propose it?
The new chair agrees to "Friday numbers" and adds: "Honestly, I didn't want to read 40 pages either." You see him smile for the first time. What do you say?
right: Thank him and get back to work

text: In the evening two directors simultaneously request the same star analyst. Each says his project will fail without her. What do you do?
The star analyst the directors are fighting over asks to meet and says: "I want to work for you directly." Flattering, but it sets a precedent. Your answer?
Someone on the leadership team leaked your internal strategy to journalists. The article has word-for-word quotes from your meeting. Six people were at the table. How do you act?
left: Talk to all of them together

text: In the evening one of the directors confesses he leaked the strategy "by accident," chatting with a journalist friend. He meant no harm. He's the best in his field. What do you do?
The press secretary proposes a rule: all directors talk to journalists only through her. Directors see it as distrust. You think it's sensible. Introduce it?
A survey shows staff describe the company as "stable," "reliable" and "boring." Marketing wants to "add some drive." How?
The agency proposes "adding drive" with daily morning exercises to music at 9 a.m. for everyone, including the CEO. You'll be on video. Take part?
The first morning workout. You mixed up left and right, and half the office copied you. The video's already in the chat. What do you do?
A month later, a new survey: staff describe the company as "stable," "reliable" and "funny." Marketing calls it a success. Do you?
Your inner voice asks in the evening: "Would you want to work at your company as a regular employee?" You think honestly. The answer: "Probably yes, if not for the meetings." What now?
The train taking you to negotiations is two hours late. Partners expect you at 11. You could do it by video from the noisy carriage with bad signal. What now?
You hold the negotiation by video from the train. Your fellow passengers listen closely. When you agree on price, they applaud. The partners on screen are baffled. What do you say?
In the evening at the station your driver holds a sign that says "CEO." Passengers turn to look. A child in the crowd asks his mom who that is. Wave to the kid?
An employee applied for an internal job in another department. Her manager objects: "I need her." She writes to you directly. Step in?
You introduce a rule: no one can block an employee's internal move for more than a month. Directors grumble: "They'll poach our people." Staff are grateful. Keep the rule?
An evening email from an employee retiring next week after 35 years: "I don't need a ceremony. Just come say goodbye." Go?
You come to say goodbye to the retiring employee. He hands you his locker key: "Thirty-five years of my work in there. You decide what to do with it." Open it?
right: Give it to the company museum

text: The retiree's locker holds notebooks logging every equipment failure for 35 years. Engineers call it "treasure." The CIO wants it digitized. How much to allocate?
At home you tell your family about the retiree's notebooks. Your kid asks: "Do you write anything down?" You only write tasks. Start a journal?
First entry in the CEO's journal: "Decided nothing today, but talked to three people who'd been waiting for it." Your assistant sees it by accident. Embarrassed?
Complaints that the canteen is too loud to talk. Facilities proposes "quiet tables" with signs. Staff laugh at the idea. Introduce it?
In the evening you decide to clear your desk. Under the papers: three invitations to events already past, and one thank-you note you never read. What now?
Your assistant preps a morning briefing: 12 items in 10 minutes. Item 7: "The CFO is in a bad mood, don't open with the budget." Useful or too much?
right: Ask her to skip the moods

text: The CFO really is in a bad mood. He admits his son failed an exam and he can't talk budgets with a smile today. What do you do?
right: Go through it fast, let him go

text: In the evening the CFO asks if you'd talk to his son "as an outsider." The son doesn't want to study economics. Neither did you, back in the day. Talk to him?
Security runs an evacuation drill. You're asked to leave the building with everyone. You're on a call with the bank. The bank's waiting. Go?
At the evacuation drill you stand outside with everyone. Staff see you for the first time without a jacket, holding coffee. They start asking questions. Twenty minutes. Answer?
right: Step away and call the bank

text: Security reports in the evening: the evacuation took 7 minutes. The last one out was the CFO, because he was "finishing a formula." What do you say to him?
left: Joke about it at the meeting

text: The facilitator asks each director to say what they dislike about the company. Everyone looks at you — is it allowed? Permit it?
At the session the CIO says he dislikes how you make decisions: "Fast, but alone." The room freezes. He's right. Your answer?
In the evening the CIO writes: "Sorry if I was harsh." You're not offended — you're grateful he said it. Your reply?
You decide the next big issue with the leadership team instead of alone. Discussion takes three hours instead of ten minutes. The outcome is better. Repeat?
A major shareholder complains decisions have slowed down. "You used to decide in ten minutes." You explain about the team. He's unimpressed. What now?
In the evening you try to square speed and teamwork. The CFO proposes a rule: "Small stuff — you decide; big stuff — together." Sounds simple. Adopt it?
A courier intern brings you documents and asks if it's true you started as a courier. You started as an analyst. But he's so hopeful. What do you say?
right: Tell him how you worked nights

text: Year-end press conference. A journalist asks: "Can you name your biggest mistake of the year?" You could name three. One involves the board. Which do you name?
After the press conference the journalist comes up: "Thanks, that was the first honest answer all day." She's writing it up. You're glad and nervous at once. What do you do?
In the morning the piece comes out: "The CEO Who Admits Mistakes." The board sends you the link with no comment. Good or bad?
The board chair says at your meeting: "Good article. But admit mistakes to us first, then to journalists." Fair. Your answer?
In the evening staff share the article in chat: "Finally, a CEO who's like us." That pleases you more than any ranking. What do you do?
Morning. For the first time in a month, not a single email before 9 a.m. Your assistant checks if email is working. It is. What do you do with the silence?
A junior analyst sends you a report; page 3 warns of a risk nobody noticed. The analyst's director hasn't read it. Praise him directly?
The risk the analyst flagged starts to materialize in the evening. Thanks to his report you have a plan. The board asks who drew it up. Name the analyst?
In the morning your old math teacher calls: "Saw you in the paper. Remember I said you'd go far?" You don't remember. Your answer?
Your teacher asks you to help the school's computer lab. The computers are 15 years old; the kids call them "dinosaurs." A small sum, but the board might ask. Help?
In the evening the school sends a photo: kids at the new computers. One boy holds a sign: "Thank you, director!" You show your family. What next?
The board proposes an open day for shareholders' families. They'll bring kids and grandkids. Security is horrified. Do it?
A major shareholder's grandson on the tour presses the red stop button on the line. The line halts. The shareholder looks at you. What do you say?
left: "Now he knows where the button is"

text: In the evening the shareholder calls, laughing: "My grandson says he wants to work for you pressing buttons." The first laugh from him in three years. Your reply?
The risk officer brings a "risk map." 140 risks, all red. Your assistant quietly asks if even one could be green. What now?
The risk officer advises you not to ride in the same car as the CFO: "key person risk." You ride together every morning to discuss the budget. Stop?
In the evening the CFO, banned from carpooling, sends a 14-minute voice message about the budget. "If we can't ride together, this'll do." Listen?
Your assistant says she sees signs of burnout: "You haven't laughed at my jokes for three days." Her jokes really are funny. Admit it?
In the middle of the day you shut your office door and stare out the window for 15 minutes. Doing nothing. Your assistant keeps everyone out. Rest or procrastination?
Friday evening. Your assistant puts an envelope on your desk: "Open on Monday." Inside: a list of what the company achieved this week without you. Care or a hint?
The CFO proposes issuing bonds with another roadshow — a "small" one this time: three cities in two days. You remember the "big" one. Agree?
Bond investors ask totally different questions than shareholders: not "how will you grow" but "how will you not go bust." For once you talk more about risks than dreams. How does it feel?
In the evening the bank reports the bonds priced below the expected rate. Savings for years. The CFO sends an emoji for the first time this year. Your reply?
HR reports call-center turnover is 60% a year. People quit after six months. She proposes a 15% raise. The CFO objects. Decision?
You sit half a day beside a call-center agent. In four hours she's been abused 11 times. She smiles into the headset every time. What do you do after the shift?
In the evening the agent you sat beside writes: "Thanks for sitting with me. Nobody upstairs knew what it's like." You stare at the message a long time. Reply?
In the morning the board approves the call-center raise but demands equal cuts elsewhere. Where do you cut?
The marketing director learns his conferences were cut for the call center. He comes to you: "Why not your trips?" Yours were already cut. Show him?
Quarterly results. Call-center turnover dropped for the first time. Customer satisfaction is up. Marketing admits the conferences "weren't that essential." Celebrate?
A big foreign company offers you its CEO job at double the pay. Moving abroad. You're 18 months into your role. Consider it?
Word of the foreign offer leaked. Directors ask: "Are you leaving?" The CFO silently updates his résumé. What do you tell the team?
In the evening you discuss the foreign offer with your family. Your kid cries: all their friends are here. Your spouse says: "Your call." Which means "don't." What do you decide?
You turn down the foreign company. The headhunter says: "Offers like this come once in a lifetime." You reply that you only get one life, too. What next?
The board learns you declined the offer. At the meeting the chair says: "We appreciate it." A week later they offer a contract extension on better terms. Accept?
right: Ask for a team bonus instead

text: In the evening the CFO confesses: he was updating his résumé because he didn't want to work for another CEO. Now he's deleting it. You feel amused and warm. What do you say?
Quarterly investor call. Just before it starts you realize the forecast slide is last year's. Three minutes to go. What now?
left: Flag it and talk it through

text: You run the call without the forecast slide. Analysts later write: "For once the CEO spoke like a human being." The stock didn't move. Ditch slides from now on?
In the evening the IR head asks for the right to check all your decks the night before. "No more last-year slides." Sensible. But one more checkpoint. Agree?
Time for the sustainability report. PR proposes a photo of you hugging a tree. You don't hug trees. Staff suggest a photo at the treatment plant. Which?
At the treatment plant they show you how it all works. An engineer proudly pours a glass of treated water and invites you to taste it. The photographer is ready. What do you do?
The sustainability report is out. The eco activists who protested a year ago write: "Not bad. Could be better." Their warmest review yet. Reply?
Every month you meet the new hires. Today one asks: "Is it true you say hello to everyone in the elevator?" It's become a legend. Your answer?
New hires swap "CEO legends." Half are true, half aren't. One says you once spent the night in the warehouse. Deny it?
In the evening you remember you really did spend a night in the warehouse when a snowstorm closed the roads. You weren't CEO yet. Tell the story?
left: Tell it at the town hall

text: Your assistant says there are no meetings before 11 a.m. today. Error or gift? She checked — a gift. What do you do until 11?
On your walk you find a department you didn't know existed. Eight people, called "Special Projects." They spend 20 minutes explaining what they do. What now?
In the evening you read the "Special Projects" report. They spent three years building a product nobody launched. It's good. Nobody remembers why it wasn't launched. What do you do?
The morning meeting opens with the sales director asking: "Does anyone know what this Special Projects department is?" Half the directors don't. Now you do. Explain?
The Special Projects product launched as a pilot. A thousand orders in a week. The sales director wants to take it over. Special Projects wants to keep running it. Who gets it?
In the evening Special Projects sends you a cake inscribed "Thanks for finding us." You share it with your assistant in the empty office. What next?
In the morning your driver says the car broke down; a replacement will take an hour. The office is a 20-minute walk. Nice weather. First call in 30 minutes. Walk?
Walking to the office, you see one of your couriers help an elderly woman carry her bags to her door. He doesn't notice you. What do you do?
left: Honor him at the town hall

text: At the evening town hall you tell the courier's story. He blushes: "It's just a normal thing." The room applauds. HR asks to set up an award. Do it?
In the morning your assistant brings coffee and the month's calendar. For the first time it has a "vacation" — a whole week nobody has claimed. She asks if it stays. Your answer?
Last day before vacation. Directors bring "a couple of two-minute questions." There are 17. Your assistant stands in the doorway holding a watch. What do you do?
First evening of vacation. You're on the shore, phone off. You catch yourself not thinking about the company for the first time in a year. Then thinking about not thinking. What next?
right: Switch the phone on for a minute

text: First morning after vacation. Your assistant greets you with a "What changed" list: a new CIO, a new coffee machine, and a new rule: "Don't disturb the CEO before 10 a.m." Who made that rule?
The new CIO asks on day one for access to everything. Including your email, "for optimization." Security tenses up. Grant it?
In the evening the new CIO sends a report: "You get 340 emails a day. 280 don't need your reply." He proposes an automatic filter. Turn it on?
A week with the email filter. You reply three times faster. But the sales director is hurt: his emails land in "no reply needed" too. Adjust it?
The sales director shows up in person: "If you won't read my emails, I'll come by." He comes five times a day. Is that worse than emails?
In the evening the CEO of your subsidiary in another city calls: "I have no one to tell I'm tired. Can I tell you?" You're his boss. But also a peer. Your reply?
You visit the subsidiary. Its CEO meets you at the station himself, no band. He says: "I figured you're tired of brass bands." Your reply?
At the subsidiary there are no meetings: decisions are made in the group chat within minutes. It works great. Your HQ directors wouldn't believe it. Adopt it?
right: It only works at small scale

text: In the evening you propose to the directors: one day a week, decide everything in chat. The CFO panics: "What about minutes?" The CIO is delighted. Try it?
First meeting-free Wednesday. By 10 a.m., 400 messages in the chat. The CFO is logging the chat in a separate spreadsheet. You've made 12 decisions by lunch. Keep it going?
The board hears about "chat Wednesdays" and demands access "for transparency." If you let them in, directors will start writing cautiously. Let them in?
In the evening you send the board Wednesday's summary: 12 decisions, zero meetings. The chair replies with one word: "Interesting." You can't tell if that's good. Ask?
Your assistant brings an odd email: an employee suggests you eat in the regular canteen "on a regular day, unannounced, to see how it really is." Go?
You eat in the canteen unannounced. A 25-minute queue, the meatballs ran out, one cashier for 300 people. Now you understand the complaints. What do you do?
right: Ask someone to sort it out

text: In the evening the canteen chef learns the CEO had buckwheat with no meatballs. He's mortified and sends a note: "Tomorrow there'll be meatballs for everyone. I promise." Reply?
The IPO investor who sent you angry emails writes again: "Shares are up 18%. I take it back. Bought some for my grandson too." Reply?
right: Forward it to the IR head

text: The analyst who once downgraded you because you looked tired upgrades to "buy." Reason: "The CEO looks well rested." How do you react?
In the evening your IR head suggests marking two years since the IPO with a dinner for the team that prepared it. Half have since moved on. Invite everyone?
An email from a former intern: he now heads a department at another company and says he still uses your advice to "say 'I don't know.'" Reply?
HR asks you to record a video for new hires: "What I wish I'd known on day one." A 15-minute shoot. You know you'll say too much. Record it?
In the evening the editor sends the video. Of your 15 minutes, 90 seconds remain — all about how you got lost in the office on day one. Approve?
right: Ask to add the strategy part

text: The board proposes widening your authority: you'll approve deals up to a set amount on your own. Faster, but the responsibility is all yours. Accept?
The first deal you approve on your own. A big sum, and you're rereading the contract for the third time. Your assistant asks if you need help. Do you?
In the evening you sign the contract. Your pen is dry. You grab your assistant's — it has a competitor's logo. Sign with it?
In the morning the cleaner you were stuck in the elevator with says she's retiring. She leaves you a list: "What to fix in the office so people feel good." 23 items. What now?
left: Fix all of it within a month

text: Item 14 on the cleaner's list: "The CEO should smile more." You read it aloud at the meeting. The directors smile. Make item 14 a rule?
Evening farewell for the cleaner. She refuses a ceremony but agrees to tea with you in the canteen. You talk for an hour. What's your parting gift?
Morning. You arrive at the office and the guard says hello first. A courier asks about your weekend. The CFO brings coffee. You realize it's just an ordinary day. How do you start it?
A newly appointed CEO at a small partner company calls: "How do you survive?" You remember your first day and your calendar until 10:45 p.m. Your advice?
Evening. You leave the office at 7 p.m. The guard says: "Early today." You say: "On time." He smiles. You get in the car. Check email?
In the morning the board chair writes: "The board is pleased. One request: find a hobby — you write to us too often." The board's first joke at your expense. Reply?
At the town hall an employee asks: "What will you do if we become the best in the industry?" The room expects something grand. Your answer?
In the evening your kid asks: "Do you like being a CEO?" For the first time you answer quickly, without hesitation. What do you say?
The board asks for a five-year strategy. You open the old one — 214 slides — and realize you need just one. Which?
The head of strategy sees your one-slide strategy: "There's nothing left for me to do." He looks lost. What do you offer him?
In the evening the board approves the one-slide strategy on one condition: add numbers. You do. Now it's two slides. Compromise?
Morning. Your assistant asks whether to keep the recurring "Meeting about meetings." Nobody attends anymore, but nobody dares delete it. Your call?
Your assistant got a promotion offer in another department. She's come for advice: go or stay. Without her it'll be rough. What do you say?
In the evening your former assistant hands over to the new one. The last instruction on her list: "Every day at 6 p.m. tell the CEO it's time to go home. There'll be arguing at first." Comply?
Monday. 40 emails, not 300. Three meetings, not thirteen. You keep looking for the catch. There isn't one. What do you do with this morning?
The sales director comes with an idea: enter a neighboring country's market. His eyes are lit up the way yours were five years ago. Back him?
right: Ask him to wait a year

text: In the evening you realize the sales director with the fire in his eyes could be a future CEO. The board asks about succession. Name him?
In the morning you tell the sales director you see him as a successor. First he's thrilled, then asks: "Is it really that hard?" Answer honestly?
You start grooming your successor. He shadows you to every meeting. Directors start turning to him instead of you. It stings a bit. Is it a good sign?
Friday evening. You sit in your office, look at the portrait with the dog and think about everything you survived this week. Tomorrow is Saturday. What now?
right: Half an hour more on email

text: In the morning the courier you once ran with brings you an invitation to his wedding. It's on Saturday. He saved all year for it, setting records. Go?
Quarterly call. At the end an analyst asks not about numbers, but about you: "How are you doing?" First time in two years. 300 people listening. Your answer?
Late evening. You reread the letter you wrote yourself on day one: "Don't forget why you came here." You remember. What do you do with the letter?
right: Put it back in the drawer

text: In the morning the new board chair invites you to speak at a CEO conference: "How Not to Burn Out at the Top." You laugh for a long time. Accept?
At the conference you say: "The secret is an assistant who sends you home, and a team you can say 'I don't know' to." Silence, then applause. What next?
Friday. 6 p.m. The new assistant stands in the doorway: "Time to go home." You want to argue. Then you remember the instructions and smile. Leave?
7:30 a.m. You arrive at the office and the cleaner — a new one now — says: "They say the last CEO never came in this early." You laugh. Full circle. Your reply?
The board announces the year's results: the company grew, turnover fell, shareholders are pleased. The chair invites you to say a few words. What do you say?
Evening, last working day of the year. Your assistant brings next year's calendar. The first week is empty. A note: "This isn't a mistake." What do you do?
In the morning your driver admits he's signed up for a coding course. In a year he might leave. He asks you not to tell HR. Your answer?
left: Support him, help with the course

text: A school class tours your office. A girl asks: "Do you have a boss?" You tell her about the board, shareholders and the chair. She nods sympathetically. Anything to add?
At a restaurant in the evening, the waiter brings the bill and asks if you're "that CEO from the eyebrow video." Nearby tables turn around. Your reply?
In the morning the shares fall 4% for the first time in a month. You notice you no longer check the chart every 40 seconds. Just once a day. Maturity or carelessness?
Staff vote for "employee of the year." Surprisingly, your assistant gets the most votes. Directors are puzzled, staff are applauding. You present the award. What do you say?
Late evening. The office is empty. You pass the "Ob" meeting room where you once waited for an intern. On the whiteboard someone wrote: "Thank you for being with us." Unsigned. Erase it?
right: Erase it before the morning meeting
